 US networks halt Trump coverage in revolt over White House ban 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — United States (US) television networks staged an extraordinary revolt Monday when they effectively boycotted coverage of President Donald Trump in protest at his decision to ban three leading outlets from the White House.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico also went to court after Trump on Friday ordered them to be barred, as the 80-year-old Republican stepped up his years-long assault on the US media.

As a result of the row, Trump’s opening of his cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the United Nations General Assembly proceeded without live television coverage.

In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said on Monday that they were halting “pool” coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.

CNN had been scheduled to serve Monday as the White House TV pool.

“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting,” ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.

The result is an almost unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press, in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting the White House.

– Media ‘like cancer’ –

There may be no live TV of Trump’s meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.

Meanwhile the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House’s website — and Trump’s comments were completely inaudible.

Several photo news organisations working at the White House, including AFP, decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organizations.

Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a “cancer” and a threat to national security.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

“It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America.”

On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel, “Trump TV,” which it said would show “top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time.”

When it went online, it was showing archive footage of Trump delivering a speech on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.

Vice President JD Vance — a former CNN commentator before his move into politics — accused the news outlets of disseminating “left-wing propaganda.”

“They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They’re just not going to get an office in the White House anymore,” he told reporters.

– Press pass confiscated –

Trump’s ban however went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.

Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.

In their lawsuit, the three organizations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the organizations said in a court filing.

A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.

Trump’s sudden announcement of the ban on Friday stunned the media — and reportedly many in his own administration.

The president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from an AFP reporter in the Oval Office on Friday that it was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years.”

Trump warned Friday that other outlets could face a similar fate, without saying which.

The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the “enemy of the people.”

But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November’s midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.

news.title: Appeals Panel Orders Use of Trump-Backed Missouri Map: What We Know
news.text: The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled in favor of a Republican-backed congressional map on Monday, saying for the upcoming midterm elections that Missouri should use the newly drawn maps, which "complies with the Constitution and federal law." In the ruling, the panel of three judges said in part, "This Court holds that Missouri’s current plan to use the 2022 map in the November 2026 general election violates the Constitution. Only use of the 2025 map complies with the Constitution and federal law. We affirm the district court and remand for entry of a permanent injunction." The decision was made by Judge James B. Loken, nominated by Republican President George H.W. Bush, Judge David R. Stras, nominated by President Donald Trump, and Judge Justin D. Smith, also nominated by Trump. The Supreme Court earlier this month granted an emergency appeal blocking the new redistricting map that would reshape Missouri's eight House districts. This ruling also came days after Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to hear an emergency appeal on the case. According to the appellate panel's ruling, the judges urged the lower court to administer a stay for one week until 5 p.m. CT September 28. "Without any stay, Secretary [of State Denny] Hoskins and local election authorities would be required to immediately begin implementing the 2025 map before the Supreme Court receives or decides any appeal." Newsweek reached out to the Supreme Court via email on Monday for comment. What To Know Stras said that he dissented in part with the decision, saying in the document in part, "There are multiple problems with this appeal. The court names one: a probable violation of Article I, section 2 of the Constitution as interpreted." The judge later added, "But I would not even get that far because People Not Politicians and Richard von Glahn lack standing. For that reason, I would dismiss the appeal." Following the 8th Circuit's decision, District Judge Stephen Clark in the Eastern District of Missouri entered a permanent injunction, ultimately blocking Hoskins or the secretary's agents, officers and employees from implementing a map other than the one from 2025. The legal wrangling has elicited uncertainty and confusion over which map voters will receive and vote on in the upcoming midterms. People Not Politicians had successfully challenged Missouri's new map, which has been celebrated by Trump, in state court and initiated the second appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court. In a previous statement to Newsweek after the High Court's ruling earlier this month, von Glahn, group executive director, said, "The law is the law, the Missouri constitution is clear as was the Missouri Supreme Court. Over 305,000 Missouri voters—Republicans, Democrats and Independents took action to block this political power grab last fall. People, not politicians, will have the final say when they vote NO on Proposition A this November." Democratic Congressman Christian Menefee of Texas also reacted to the panel's decision on Monday, saying on X, "This is outrageous. The Supreme Court already stepped in twice to block Missouri's rigged map. Ballots are already in the mail. Now, at the 11th hour, an appeals court is letting Missouri Republicans force that rigged map on voters anyway. All to erase a Kansas City district and silence Black and Brown voters. Catastrophic for confidence in our elections." What This New Decision Means Absentee ballots have been shipped out to military voters and overseas citizens with the 2022 maps. By Tuesday, absentee ballots are to be available to all other voters under state law, according to the Associated Press. In the panel's decision, the judges argued in part, "For all Missouri voters not covered by UOCAVA [Uniformed and Overseas Citizens Absentee Voting Act], absentee ballots may be requested and cast beginning on September 22, 2026. Mo. Rev. Stat. § 115.281.1. That deadline has not yet arrived, and thus general absentee voting has not yet begun. Accordingly, the September 22, 2026, absentee ballot commencement date does not moot this case." Neama Rahmani, former federal prosecutor and the president of West Coast Trial Lawyers, told Newsweek via email on Monday night, "Missouri is a total mess. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 map was unlawful because it was not approved by the voters. Normally a state Supreme Court is the ultimate decision maker when it comes to state law, but now a federal circuit court has ruled that changing back to old 2022 map violates federal law because congressional districts can't be changed between primary and general elections." Rahmani continued, "There is also a reverse-Purcell issue, with the federal appellate court holding that the new 2025 map is effectively the status quo and should not be changed shortly before an election. The problem is some ballots have already been mailed and a number of Missourians have voted. Had the Missouri Secretary of State simply put the issue of the new map to the voters instead of deciding that it was legally unnecessary, we wouldn't be in the mess. Instead, the U.S. Supreme Court will almost certainly have to step in and resolve this dispute between state and federal law." Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. For questions on this story, contact Newsweek editor Edward T. Cummins.
news.summary: The legal back and forth has created uncertainty regarding which map voters will receive and vote on in the midterms.

news.title: Tech rally boosts Asian stocks, dollar firms on rate-hike wagers
news.text:
SINGAPORE: Technology stocks powered Asian markets higher on Tuesday as lower oil prices lifted sentiment and investors ​pinned their hopes on US-Iran talks, while the dollar stood tall on bets that more hikes are needed to rein ‌in inflation.

Attention is also turning to a high-stakes meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping later this week, with investors watching for signs the leaders of the world’s two largest economies can prevent a further deterioration in relations.

Xi arrives in Washington on Wednesday for the first time in more than a decade amid growing optimism that ​a trade truce deal between the two nations will be extended and potential cooperation over artificial intelligence.

Brent crude futures steadied at $100.22 per ​barrel after dropping over 3% in the previous session, moving below the key $100 level briefly.

President Trump said he ⁠would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is expected to be in New York this week for the UN General Assembly, ​helping lift sentiment and pushing bond yields lower.

“The drop in oil is a big factor,” said Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global. “Oil is ​the main driver and investors are jumping back into AI as has been the pattern this year.”

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rose over 1% in early trading. Tech-heavy South Korean stocks jumped nearly 2% while Taiwan shares were 1.3% higher. Japan markets are closed for a holiday.

Nasdaq futures rose 0.37% while European ​futures were 0.3% higher. Much of the AI enthusiasm has been centred on the strong reception to the launch of Meta’s Muse AI assistant.

China’s ​blue-chip stock index rose 0.75%, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index gained 0.4%. AI stocks in China and Hong Kong also surged.

“The excitement around Meta Muse is ‌adding weight ⁠to the idea that millions of people could eventually use persistent AI agents,” said Chris Weston, head of research at Pepperstone.

“The combination of Meta Muse injecting a new shot of confidence in the CPU demand profile, lower crude prices, falling Treasury yields and optimism towards the US-China summit have supported the move.”

Rate hikes on the way

Investors are also contending with a fresh wave of rate hikes and hawkish signals from major central banks, reinforcing ​expectations of further tightening later this ​year. The shift has underpinned ⁠the dollar and piled pressure on the yen.

The yen was at 157.39 per US dollar, hovering near a three-week low after surrendering early-month gains driven by bets on a faster pace of Bank of Japan rate ​hikes.

The BOJ raised rates last week to a 31-year high but two dissenting votes and lack of explicit ​hawkish guidance disappointed ⁠investors, leaving the yen vulnerable and stoking intervention jitters.

“FX intervention remains a blunt tool to prop up currencies, and without a forceful monetary policy response it will be difficult for Japanese authorities to rein in the selloff in the yen,” said Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at Ebury.

The Federal Reserve, by ⁠contrast, raised ​rates last week and warned its fight against inflation was not over, keeping the ​door open to further tightening.

The dollar index , which measures the US currency against six other units, was at 100.4, just shy of a seven-week high. Traders are pricing in a ​56% chance of a hike in October, compared with 43.5% a week earlier, CME FedWatch tool showed.

news.title: Trump delivered a speech at this event. But you can't hear what he said
news.text:
Standing on the White House lawn, US President Donald Trump showed off his new granite helicopter pad.

He used oversized gold scissors to cut a red, white and blue ribbon, and exchanged handshakes with the construction crew.

He had some words to mark the occasion on Monday, local time, but without a microphone in front of him, they did not reach many ears.

Usually, this sort of moment would be captured by the White House press pool.

But days after the president escalated his attacks on American media outlets, the pool reporters were not there.

"Maybe … this is one example of it backfiring just a little bit," a Newsmax presenter watching a silent feed remarked.

Here is how the president got here.

First, catch me up

The president announced on Friday that he had banned three prominent media outlets from the White House, blocking them from serving as White House pool representatives. 

Cable networks CNN and MS Now, and online publisher Politico, were barred "effective immediately" because of their "constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS", Mr Trump told his Truth Social followers.

He threatened further bans of other media outlets would follow.

Reporters from all three were denied entrance to the White House grounds the next day.

What is the White House pool?

A press pool is when a group of news organisations combine their resources to gather and distribute notes, news, photos and video.

They are created when space at, or access to, an event is limited.

For example, Australian media organisations are currently part of a press pool to share footage of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on his US trip for the United Nations General Assembly.

The White House press pool covers the US president every day.

The television arm is made up of five networks: The American ABC News, CBS News, NBC News, CNN and Fox News.

They use a rotating schedule to cover the president's movements and share the footage with each other and affiliates.

What does the ban look like in practice?

There has been a wider knock-on effect.

The remainder of the White House television pool announced it would suspend coverage of Mr Trump.

CNN was scheduled to be the television network pool representative for Mr Trump's trip to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Monday, local time, but was unable to fulfil the commitment due to the ban.

But the pool said it would not send a back-up crew.

It meant there was little to no live video footage of the president's trip captured by independent news media.

The suspension also led to Mr Trump's unveiling of the new White House helipad going largely unheard.

How did Trump respond?

On Truth Social, Mr Trump insisted the ban was not an attack on press freedom.

"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," he wrote.

Speaking to reporters in New York after a meeting with Mayor Zohran Mamdani, he tried to shrug off the lack of network television coverage of his movements.

"It's interesting because they said they were gonna boycott me. But they never boycott me," he said. 

"I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair."

Is Trump really allowed to deny journalists access?

That is something the courts will need to decide.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico are suing the administration over the ban, which they say denies their First Amendment rights to free speech.

The US Constitution guarantees a free press, stating the government "shall make no law … abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press".

But the Trump administration insists the First Amendment protects the right to publish but does not entitle the media to a White House pass, briefing room seat or place in the press pool.

Last year, the Trump administration up-ended a decades-long tradition of the White House Correspondents Association, which operates independently of the government, selecting journalists for the pool.

Instead, the White House now picks and chooses which members of the media make up the pool.
news.summary: Days after the president escalated his attacks on American media outlets, Donald Trump's words at a ribbon cutting ceremony for a new helicopter pad on the White House lawn went largely unheard.

news.title: Houthis push for control of Yemen’s highlands
news.text:
Trump speaks with Yemen’s president, doesn’t pledge military support• NYT says US president reversed decision on air strikes on Houthis

DUBAI: Houthi fighters were pushing to seize strategic heights in Yemen on Monday to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces, after a report that President Donald Trump had called off US strikes on the group at the last minute.

US President Trump spoke by phone with Yem-eni President Rashad al-Alimi on Sun-day, four people familiar with the matter said, discussing the advances of the Houthis around a vital global waterway.

Alimi requested US support for his Saudi-backed government in its fight against the Houthis, who this month took key areas along the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive.

Two of the sources, one Yemeni and one Western, said Trump had made no direct pledge of military support during the call. The White House and Yemen’s information minister did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

On the other hand, a lightning advance by the Houthis this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre.

Strategic heights

Five Yemeni military sources told Reu-ters that the Houthis were now seeking to seize strategic heights, known as the Kah-b-oub Mountains, in two provinces, Taiz and Lahij, which separate the Red Sea coast from the government-held south.

Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote mountain Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province, and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast between the mouth of the Red Sea that the fighters captured last week and the government’s base in Aden.

The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab Strait leading into the Red Sea by taking control of the heights, which would allow them to open new fronts, according to the sources. That would help protect exposed positions the Houthis captured during their advance around Dhubab on the Red Sea and on Perim Island in the strait.

The Houthis, who have controlled Yemen’s capital since 2014, seized the country’s Red Sea coast this month in a lightning advance that routed forces of an internationally recognised Yemeni government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia and based in the south.

The New York Times reported that President Trump has changed his strategy on Yemen several times, torn betw-een Saudi pressure to strike the Iran-backed Houthis and the risk of opening another front in the Middle East war.

It said Saudi Crown Prince Moham-med bin Salman called Trump on Sun-day “to implore him, again, to step in to help blunt the rapidly advancing group”.

Trump had told his advisers the day before that he opposed strikes but chan-ged his mind after the call and “told the Pentagon to prepare for air strikes agai-nst the Houthis”, the newspaper repor-t-ed, citing anonymous administration officials.

However, he appeared to have reve-rsed his decision again by midday Sunday, it said.

Trump’s decision to pull back from striking the Houthis came as “commanders had approved target lists, troops were loading bombs onto US warplanes selected for the missions and the wave of attacks was just about to begin”, the Times said, citing two people briefed on the operation.

US news platform Axios said Trump had already refused a Saudi request to strike the Houthis last week. Fox News reported on Sunday that Trump had said the Houthis have agreed not to hit US targets.

news.title: Oil rises slightly ahead of potential US-Iran talks
news.text:
Oil prices gained on Tuesday as the market steadied after several days of declines, with investors awaiting developments on potential US-Iran talks at the United Nations General ​Assembly this week.

The Brent crude futures November contract gained 22 cents, or 0.22%, ‌to $100.57 a barrel at 0021 GMT.

The WTI October contract, which expires on Tuesday, crept up 2 cents, or 0.02%, to $95.8 a barrel.

The more actively traded November contract was up 13 cents, or 0.14%, ​at $92.49 a barrel.

Iran and the US exchanged threats on Sunday, though President Donald Trump ​said he would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who ⁠is expected to be in New York this week for the UN General Assembly.

“The move ​higher in WTI and the stronger open in Brent have the appearance of a typical ​short-covering bounce after the recent decline, rather than a fundamental shift,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

“Traders who were positioned for further downside are taking some risk off the table while the ​diplomatic narrative plays out.”

Over the weekend, Iran also conveyed its conditions to mediators for ​re-engaging in negotiations, Al Jazeera reported, citing Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.

Waterer added that prices were likely ‌to remain ⁠range-bound and sensitive to headlines until there was either clear progress or a setback in diplomatic efforts between the United States and Iran.

Middle East tensions remained elevated after Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked Riyadh and a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu and stepped up efforts ​to cut off ​Saudi-backed forces from the ⁠Red Sea coast.

China has privately urged Tehran to help curb attacks by the Houthis, three Iranian sources said, after Saudi Arabia appealed to ​Beijing following a recent surge in the group’s military operations.

Aramco has ​increased exports ⁠through the Strait of Hormuz after attacks on its East-West Pipeline forced it to halt some shipments through Yanbu.

Saudi Aramco loaded about 14 million barrels of crude oil on seven supertankers ⁠inside the ​Gulf on Sunday, tanker tracking data showed.

Separately, Libya’s National ​Oil Corp Chairman Massoud Suleman told Reuters on Monday that the country’s Sharara oilfield has seen a partial reduction ​in production, without giving a reason.

news.text:
Naqvi meets Pezeshkian, Momeni to ‘discuss mediation process’• Iran ‘grateful’ to Pakistan’s political, military leadership for peace efforts• US refuses visas to some members of Iranian president’s delegation• Second Qatari LNG cargo ship ‘cleared by Iranians’ due today

ISLAMABAD: Iran on Monday indicated its willingness to return to dialogue with the United States to de-escalate tensions. The flexibility on the issue was indicated by the Iranian side during a meeting between Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who is in the Iranian capital in an attempt to revive the stalled diplomatic process between Washington and Tehran.

“Yes, there was progress during the meeting,” a source told Dawn. Mr Naqvi, who arrived in Tehran on Monday, was received by his Iranian counterpart Eskandar Momeni. “We had discussions on the mediation process,” Mr Naqvi said while talking to media in the presence of his Iranian counterpart.

During the meeting, Mr Momeni said Iran was thankful to Pakistan’s political and military leadership for its efforts for regional peace and stability. “We are grateful to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir for their efforts for regional peace,” the Iranian minister was quoted as saying in a statement issued here by the interior ministry.

The visit comes at a time when diplomatic activity has intensified to prevent another round of escalation between Iran and US, with both Qatar and Pakistan maintaining contacts with the two sides.

Qatar has in recent we--eks emerged as a key channel between Wa--sh-ing-ton and Tehran. Its foreign ministry said on Monday that its mediation team had been exchanging ideas with both sides for nearly two weeks in an effort to bridge differences and find a suitable moment to resume negotiations.

Iran relays conditions for talks

Iran has conveyed through Qatar a set of conditions for reopening talks, including an end to fighting on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian assets and an end to the US naval blockade. Iranian officials said seven conditions were conveyed, although all of them were not publicly disclosed.

The latest diplomatic activity follows the collapse of the 14 point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding brokered by Pakistan on June 17. The conflict has since continued with sporadic strikes and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports, while Iran has maintained control over traffic through the strategic waterway.

Pakistan, meanwhile, has remained engaged in efforts to keep the diplomatic channel open. Field Marshal Asim Munir has used his contacts with the US administration while Pakistani officials have made repeated visits to Tehran.

The latest visit also carries significance ahead of Mr Pezeshkian’s travel to New York for the United Nations General Assembly. The Iranian president is expected to meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on the sidelines of the UNGA in the coming days. The meeting could provide another opportunity for the two leaders to discuss the stalled peace process.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has given mixed signals on the prospects of renewed negotiations, while Ira-nian officials have continued to combine their readiness for diplomacy with warnings of a strong response to any fresh US military action.

The possibility of renewed diplomacy is also being backed by developments around the Strait of Hormuz, where Pakistan has quietly secured the passage of another Qatari liquefied natural gas shipment after negotiations with Iran.

The shipment crossed the strait over the weekend and is expected to reach Pakistan’s LNG import facility by Tuesday, making it the second Qatari LNG cargo to reach Pakistan this month through an understanding with Iran.

No visa from US

Separately, the US refu-sed to issue visas to members of President Pezesh-kian’s delegation, including his communications team, for his trip to the UN General Assembly, Iranian state media reported. President Peze-shkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to enter the United States since the Middle East war began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, part of the delegation to the UN, left Iran on Sunday evening for a stopover in Qatar.

Foreign ministry spok-esman Esmaeil Baqaei accused the Trump administration of “trampling on the right of access to information”, pointing to its recent move to bar three major US media outlets from the White House over objections to their coverage.

“When an administration slams its doors shut — even on American journalists it happens to dislike — and bars foreign reporters, including the Iranian president’s media team, whose voices it would rather silence, it is not managing access; it is trying to hide the truth,” Baqaei said on X.

Iranian airlines to be ‘shut down’ from tomorrow

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Iranian airlines will have trouble functioning globally in two days under the weight of American sanctions. On Sept 23, “all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world,” Bessent told CNBC in an interview as the war launched by the United States and Israel nears the seven-month mark.

“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” he added.Two Iraqi sources told AFP on Monday that Baghdad would suspend flights by Iranian airlines following the US Treasury’s announcement.

Georgia also barred Iranian carriers from its land, while Iranian airline Mahan said it suspended service to Turkiye at the re--quest of the Turkish government.

news.title: Gold muted as higher-for-longer rate outlook weighs
news.text:
Gold ​prices struggled for momentum on Tuesday as expectations of interest rates staying ‌higher for longer weighed on sentiment, with investors awaiting comments from US Federal Reserve officials for policy clues.

Spot gold was little changed at $4,344.29 per ounce, as of 0151 GMT.

US gold futures ​steadied at $4,381.80.

Bullion is traditionally viewed as a hedge against inflation and geopolitical ​risks, but its appeal tends to wane in a high-interest-rate environment as ⁠investors favour yield-bearing assets.

With US economic data limited this week, investors will focus ​on comments from Fed officials for signs of whether the central bank is leaning toward ​another rate increase in October, as well as on crude oil prices, said Chris Weston head of research at Pepperstone.

“While crude has come modestly off its recent highs, a reversal higher that ​builds inflation expectations would only intensify the rates story, and gold would likely continue ​to face headwinds,” said Weston.

The Fed raised its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage ‌point ⁠last week and flagged more hikes in the coming months.

The US central bank will likely need to hike rates further to lower inflation resulting from strong demand as well as a commodity price shock that has moved beyond oil, St. Louis Fed President Alberto ​Musalem said, adding ​that it would be ⁠better for the Fed to act sooner than wait.

On the geopolitical front, Houthi fighters pushed to seize strategic heights in Yemen to ​cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held ​by Saudi-backed ⁠forces, after a report that US President Donald Trump had called off American strikes on the group at the last minute.

Oil prices gained as the market steadied after several days ⁠of ​declines, with investors awaiting developments on potential US-Iran talks ​at the United Nations General Assembly this week.

Spot silver rose 0.3% to $66.19, platinum gained 0.3% to $1,792.76 and palladium ​climbed 0.3% to $1,305.10.

news.title: Trump makes unusual visit to New York Mayor Mamdani's residence
news.text: Digital Desk | New York, Sep 22 (IANS) Donald Trump made an unusual visit for a sitting president to the official residence of the city's mayor for a meeting with Zohran Mamdani. The visit, marked by bonhomie, came as a surprise on Monday because Mamdani is a Democratic Socialist, while Trump has made attacks on socialists a running theme of his campaign for Republican candidates in the midterm elections. And Mamdani had called Trump a "fascist". It was Trump's first appointment in the city after he arrived there for the United Nations high-level week. After their meeting, Trump praised Mamdani, saying he was "off to a good start" and was "going to be a great" mayor. The populists from the two ends of the political spectrum appear to have hit it off despite their ideological differences and their belligerent bases, and this was the first time in 44 years a president has visited the city's mayor at his residence. They appeared to have bonded over their interest in building structures. Mamdani has proposed a massive housing complex with 12,000 housing units built on top of a rail yard. “What we’re talking about is something very rare in our city; it’s the possibility of constructing an entirely new neighbourhood,” Mamdani said at their news conference. He said it would require federal assistance. Recognising the nationwide housing shortage, Trump has proposed plans to ameliorate it. Mamdani said that he aired his opposition to Trump's policies, including the immigration crackdown and the withdrawal of temporary immigration status given to people from countries in turmoil like Haiti. "I shared my very strong opinions about how we can keep New Yorkers safe, how we can keep immigrant New Yorkers safe", Mamdani said. Trump said Mamdani felt “very strongly” about the issue. Despite their differences, Trump, a native New Yorker, said he had seen "numerous different mayors ... some great ones and some not so great ones". "I'll be able to say you’re going to be a great one, and you’re off to a start", he said. A reporter asked Mamdani about Trump banning reporters from CNN and MS Now networks, and Politico news outlet. He said, “I told the president that we’re going to have all of the members of the press here on the lawn and that is something that I believe in.” Pointing to the presence of the media, Trump said, "It's interesting 'cause they said they were gonna boycott me, but they never boycott me. So, I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press". He accused the media of propagating "fake news" and said he had an "obligation" to keep them out. Mamdani and Trump had earlier met in February at the White House, which was also marked by surprising friendliness. According to Politico, true to his socialist roots, Mamdani was scheduled to meet Bernie Sanders, the leftist senator and vehement critic of Trump, who has been like a mentor to him. The mayor's 15-room residence set on 4.5 hectares along the East River is officially known as Gracie Mansion. Trump, who has an eye for decor and architecture, called it “a beautiful place" and had said earlier on Truth Social that he had visited the mansion several times before becoming president.

news.title: Trump launches state-run TV 'like North Korea' after being humiliated by press boycott
news.text: US President Donald Trump has announced he is launching his own TV channel after an awkward on-camera moment caused by a press boycott. The boycott is in effect after the US President banned a number of media outlets from the White House grounds. The 47th President of the United States appeared at a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new White House helipad, but as the usual television press pool had been banned by the Trump administration, Trump seemingly spoke into the void as viewers back home had no audio of what he was saying. CNN, Politico, and MS NOW had their press credentials revoked at the weekend by the Trump administration after the US President accused them of unfavourable and "fake" coverage. Without a press pool, there was no network of microphones positioned nearby to ensure Trump's words were captured. Trump's words were drowned out by significant background noise. Newsmax aired footage of the bizarre incident, showing the knock-on effect of Trump's media ban for all to see. Host Bianca de la Garza explained: "There's no microphone because the pool cameras aren't there." She added to her co-host: "Maybe, Tim, this is one example of it backfiring just a little bit. “Obviously, the ramifications are right here. Can't hear what the president's saying." Just days after President Donald Trump barred various media outlets from the White House, the Trump administration has launched its own 24-hour television channel, called 'Trump TV'. The new service launched Monday night at around 7 pm ET, as per a statement from the White House itself. The state-run media channel appears to run a constant feed of the Trump administration's “biggest moments all in one place". The first piece of footage shared on America's new state-run media channel was a two-month-old speech that Trump made at Mount Rushmore, back on July 3. Deputy assistant to the President, Kaelan Dorr, described the network on X as a "livestream of the Administration’s greatest hits, unfiltered." On X, the White House described the channel as "24/7 [coverage] updated in real time, with top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place." The post ended on: "Not every big moment has made it on your TV; now it can." The removal of the free press from the White House grounds, as well as the new state-run media channel, were quick to draw comparisons to Kremlin propaganda channels in Russia and state-run, heavily censored TV in North Korea. On X, one user painted a fairly obvious picture to recap recent events: "The Trump administration announces state-run media, similar to Russia and North Korea, launching 'Trump TV', its own 24/7 streaming channel of the administration's remarks and events, going live tonight at 7 p.m. [local time] and claiming 'just the news that matters most - straight from the Trump Administration.' "This is the first time in US history an American president has launched a formal state-media channel in his own name. It comes three days after the White House banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and hours after the five-network TV pool stopped covering Trump's events in response, leaving a White House event today with video but no sound. "The White House is now broadcasting the President itself." Another X user added: "We’re now at the “state-run media” stage of Trump’s authoritarian takeover."
news.summary: Trump revoked the press credentials for a number of media outlets, effectively banning them from the White House grounds. Days later, his adminstraistration launched the US-first ever stat run media channel
news.author: Rachel Vickers-Price

news.title: As leaders meet in New York, the fate of the world may rest on Trump and Xi
news.text:
In coming days, presidents and prime ministers from an estimated 130 countries will come together in New York.

But during this time there will be only one meeting that could determine the immediate fate of the world: that will be in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

For the leaders gathering in New York at the United Nations General Assembly, there are of course major issues to be discussed: a suddenly expressed panic over artificial intelligence (AI), the Iran war and its resulting crisis in the world energy market, erratic immigration flows and climate change being among them.

On the Iran war, the reality is that Trump is unable to end it. It takes two to end a war, and at this moment the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) which runs Iran does not want the conflict to end.

The IRGC wants to inflict as much political punishment as possible on Trump for what they believe have been unjustified attacks on their infrastructure and civilians. These attacks include the suspected US strikes on an Iranian school that killed 120 school children, an attack which the UN last week determined could amount to a war crime.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian will address the UN on the home turf of the country it remains at war with, while at the same time, the US has blocked Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas from attending the same summit designed to be a global gathering to promote international peace.

This alone is extraordinary, the United States is allowing the leader of a country with which it is at war to enter New York while preventing the leader of the moderate faction of the Palestinians from attending, for the second consecutive year.

Abbas's Palestinian Authority is a bitter opponent of Hamas, and for years American officials have wanted the moderates to be embraced as part of trying to find a way towards a two-state solution.

But now not even a moderate Palestinian leader is allowed into the US.

China challenging the supremacy of the US

As is increasingly the case in this new world order, China is likely to prove yet again to be a key player.

It was China who brought together Iran and Saudi Arabia in Beijing three years ago to encourage them to drop the ancient Shia-Sunni rivalry, so it is China who could mediate between the US and Iran. But only if it so chooses.

So far, China's economy has not been badly impacted by the Iran war as it has enormous oil and petrol reserves.

But should the war drag into next year, as many in Washington expect it might, then China will have a real reason to pressure Iran to end the war because by then, its own oil reserves will start to diminish. China has a much greater ability to bring an end to this war than the US.

That is yet another indication that China is challenging the supremacy of the US in international matters.

China has tended to be reluctant to get involved in international conflicts but when self interest is involved, it reconsiders.

When the UN General Assembly met last year, the world was a very different place. Since then, the BRICS trade alliance — consisting of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa — has become much stronger.

Xi told the BRICS meeting in New Delhi recently: "China is willing to work with fellow BRICS members to play a role in achieving peace and stability in the Middle East and the Gulf region."

And separately, South Korea, Japan and China have begun discussing a new trade pact.

China is skipping UNGA this year, with Xi heading directly to Washington to meet with Trump.

A year of change in the US and abroad

Another major change since last year is that Iran has managed to close the Strait of Hormuz, affecting 20 per cent of the world's energy flows.

In addition, the Iran-allied Houthis in Yemen have shown they, too, can jeopardise the flow of oil through the Red Sea.

And since last year, traditional US allies Saudi Arabia and Canada have had a rude awakening.

In the past fortnight, Trump reportedly twice has rejected Saudi requests for military assistance against the Houthis. In effect, he told Saudi Arabia that when it comes to their military battle against the Houthis they are on largely on their own, with the exception of some shared intelligence.

And in terms of Canada, historically one of America's closest allies, in recent weeks Trump has declared a full-scale trade war against a country which is the major trading partner for 25 American states.

In another shift since last year, the attitudes of many countries, including the US, have hardened against Israel. While the White House continues to support Israel, the attitudes of the American public have turned.

Surveys by both the Pew Research Centre and Gallop show there is now more support in the US for Palestinians than there is for Israelis.

Added to this, US Vice-President JD Vance has recently warned the US is the "only powerful ally" Israel has left in the world.

Europe warned 'no-one is safe' from Russia

In terms of Europe, since last year European countries have begun examining the possibility of a NATO alliance without the US.

Countries such as Poland are also now on heightened alert for a military attack by Russia.

French President Emmanuel Macron warned recently of the risk of Russian hybrid warfare in Europe.

"The nature of Russian aggression and threats in Europe is changing," the president said during a security briefing last Friday. "No-one is safe."

The "Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and France has intensified", he added.

And finally, a war that Trump once said he could solve within 24 hours, Ukraine, is worsening.

French media is reporting that in a single night late last week, there were as many as 138 drone or cyber attacks by Russia on neighbouring countries other than Ukraine, including Estonia and Poland.

All of these crises rage while conflicts in Gaza, Sudan, Myanmar and the Congo continue, raising the question of the UN's efficacy to end global conflicts.

So while leaders from 130 countries grapple with all of these changes, in Washington, Trump and Xi will sit down. If they were able to come to an agreement, these two could address key issues such as AI and the Iran and Ukraine wars.

But given the fierce competition between the two, few people are expecting that to be the case.
news.summary: A lot has changed since last year's United Nations General Assembly while conflicts in the Middle East, Sudan, Myanmar and the Congo continue, raising the question of the UN's efficacy to end global conflicts.
news.author: John Lyons

news.title: White House launches ‘Trump TV.’ What is it?
news.text:
The White House has launched a round-the-clock livestream dubbed “TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station,” featuring presidential speeches, announcements and curated administration highlights amid an escalating dispute with several major US news organizations.

The stream went live at 7pm ET on Monday on the official White House YouTube channel. Rather than a new television network or standalone streaming service, Trump TV is essentially a continuous YouTube broadcast compiling existing and new administration footage.

Its official description promises the administration’s “biggest moments,” alongside top videos, major remarks and other highlights. The stream runs around the clock and is updated in real time. The broadcast opened with a recording of President Donald Trump’s speech at Mount Rushmore marking the 250th anniversary of the United States.

Where can it be watched?

Trump TV can be watched for free through the official White House YouTube channel. The same feed is also embedded on the White House website. No separate subscription, television provider or dedicated app is required.

The initiative comes days after Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters and photographers from White House grounds, accusing the outlets of repeatedly publishing “fake news.”

CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed a federal lawsuit on Monday seeking to overturn the restrictions. The outlets say the ban amounts to unconstitutional retaliation for critical coverage and viewpoint discrimination and argue that their credentials were revoked without notice or due process.

How did US media react?

The dispute prompted an unusual show of solidarity among major television networks. After CNN was prevented from carrying out its scheduled duties as the designated White House pool broadcaster, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC suspended their participation in pooled television coverage.

The networks said the public has a “vital interest” in receiving independent information about the government and argued that administrations should not restrict news organizations because they object to their reporting.

What happened without the TV pool?

Under the pool system, television networks take turns providing a camera crew, microphones and a shared feed from presidential events that other broadcasters can use.

The effects of the TV pool suspension were immediately visible during Monday’s unveiling of a new presidential helipad. Viewers of the official feed could see Trump speaking but could not properly hear his remarks because the television pool’s boom microphone was absent.

Print, radio and wire pool reporting continued, while several organizations also withheld photography and other visual coverage.

How has the administration responded?

Trump responded on Truth Social by doubling down on his criticism of the organizations and suggesting his administration would appeal an unfavorable ruling.

The administration has defended the restrictions, arguing that while the First Amendment protects the media’s right to publish, it does not guarantee a permanent press pass, briefing-room seat or place in the press pool.
news.summary:
The White House has launched a round-the-clock livestream amid an escalating dispute with major US media outlets

news.title: UK and US make first-ever torpedo test from uncrewed vessel
news.text:
Britain and the United States have for the first time test-fired a torpedo from an uncrewed undersea vessel rather than a crewed submarine, the UK government announced Monday.

London said in a statement the live firing took place in UK waters last week as part of the AUKUS alliance with Australia.

The British government said the test "marks a major advance in the future of submarine technology" for the three countries.

It "delivers a significant breakthrough for Euro-Atlantic security and NATO's undersea advantage", the statement added.

Western countries are rushing to modernise their war-fighting capabilities with autonomous systems, in the face of threats from Russia and Iran.

London said the heavyweight torpedo -- jointly developed by the US and Australia -- was launched from a 12-metre (40-ft) long undersea drone manufactured in Britain and named Excalibur.

Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at the RUSI think-tank, called the development "noteworthy".

"The employment of a lethal payload illustrates that uncrewed systems can play roles which extend beyond surveillance," he told AFP.

The announcement came as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham headed to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.

Burnham is due to have his first meeting with US President Donald Trump at the summit since becoming UK leader in July.

The UK government said that Burnham would use his trip to New York to "drive forward global work" on artificial intelligence.

He will announce "a new AI and autonomy partnership" with the US that will "help the UK protect critical national infrastructure, from sea lanes to air space", the statement added.

"This week I will be making the case for closer international cooperation on AI, a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, and renewed efforts to bring an end to the conflict in the Middle East because what happens abroad impacts each and every one of us at home," said Burnham.

He confirmed that Britain would host the G20 summit in November 2027 in the northwestern English city of Manchester.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
news.summary: The United Kingdom and the United States have for the first time test-fired a torpedo from an uncrewed underwater vessel, marking a step forward in AUKUS efforts to develop autonomous naval technology.

news.title: World News | Iran Foreign Minister Araghchi Arrives in New York to Participate in 81st UNGA Session
news.text:
New York [US], September 22 (ANI): Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi arrived in New York on Monday (local time) to participate in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), Iran's state-run news agency IRNA reported. 

Araghchi is expected to hold consultations on the latest regional developments during the UNGA High-Level Week.

His arrival comes as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will also travel to New York on Tuesday to participate in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, representing the Islamic Republic amid ongoing conflict and tensions with the United States, Iranian state media IRNA reported.

According to IRNA, Iranian presidential official Abbasi told the agency that Pezeshkian is scheduled to leave for New York on Tuesday to attend the UN General Assembly.

Also Read | JD Vance Defends Donald Trump's White House Media Ban as CNN, MS NOW and Politico Sue.

During his visit, Pezeshkian is expected to address the UN General Assembly and outline Iran's positions on international developments, particularly on the matter of the US-Israeli war of aggression imposed against Iran, IRNA reported.

Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Wednesday, September 23, during the morning session. The Iranian President is also expected to hold meetings and consultations with leaders and senior officials from several countries on the sidelines of the UNGA.

Pezeshkian's programme in New York will also include meetings with educated Iranians living in the United States, as well as discussions with American elites and think tanks.

A high-ranking Iranian delegation will accompany the President during the visit.

IRNA also reported that the US government has denied visas to some members of the high-ranking Iranian delegation, including members of the President's media team, describing it as an unprecedented hostile action by Washington.

The 81st session of the UN General Assembly is being held under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations That Delivers for All.”

The high-level general debate is scheduled to take place from September 22-26 and on September 28 in New York, with world leaders expected to discuss major international challenges.

The session's agenda also includes high-level meetings on climate action, development, sea-level rise, pandemic preparedness and other global issues. 

The Iran delegation's arrival comes at a time when United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that Iranian airlines could be effectively shut out of international travel from Wednesday (local time), on September 23, as Washington threatens secondary sanctions against foreign companies that continue providing services to Iran’s carriers.

According to Al Jazeera, Bessent said on Monday that “on September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world,” as the Trump administration steps up economic pressure on Tehran.

The warning extends beyond Iranian airlines to foreign airports, fuel suppliers, ticketing companies and other businesses involved in supporting the carriers’ international operations.

“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said, according to Al Jazeera.

The latest threat came amid the Trump administration’s broader sanctions campaign aimed at restricting Iran’s access to international financial and commercial networks. (ANI)

news.title: US to open two new military bases in Greenland — Reuters
news.text:
WASHINGTON, September 22. /TASS/. The United States intends to start using two more military bases in Greenland under a deal to be signed with Denmark, Reuters reported.

The US "plans to re-establish a Cold War-era military base in southern Greenland and set up another on the east , now used by the Danish dog sled patrol," the agency said, citing sources. The sites are Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Bluie West One military base in the 1950s, and Mestersvig, a ·military outpost currently used by a Danish special forces unit, ·according to the publication.

Denmark, Greenland and the United States are to sign their new agreement at the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22, the report said. US President Donald Trump said earlier that the US and Denmark had agreed to transfer control over Greenland’s security to Washington, adding that the US side would immediately begin ramping up its military presence on the Arctic island.

A major topic at Monday's meeting was the proposed redevelopment of Sunnyside Yard in Queens.  Paramount settles with US states to clear Warner Bros. mega-merger 







LOS ANGELES, United States (AFP) — Paramount has reached a settlement with a group of US states that clears the way for its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, officials announced Monday, creating a Hollywood empire spanning television, news and cinema.

Paramount, which is run by David Ellison, whose ultra-wealthy family has ties to US President Donald Trump, won a bidding war against Netflix in February for control of a stable of assets that includes Warner Bros. Pictures, CNN and the HBO Max streaming service.

The Trump administration approved the deal, one of the largest media mergers in years, in June without demanding a change to its business, before 12 US states sued to block the transaction.

Financing for the deal reportedly includes about $24 billion in equity from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. David Ellison’s father, billionaire Oracle founder Larry Ellison, also provided funding and a guarantee.

Opponents in the movie industry said the combined company would slash jobs in a Hollywood already under pressure and reduce the number of films produced every year, while news media groups feared CNN’s independence could be compromised.

The deal includes several safeguards on these issues, including a board meant to protect CNN’s editorial independence.

The news comes just days after Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House. The outlets are suing the administration to have the decision reversed.

Paramount had threatened to move out of California if the state’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, did not negotiate an end to the lawsuit.

In their complaint, the 12 states argued the combined company would control roughly 27 percent of wide-release theatrical film distribution and a similar percentage of the basic cable channel industry.

California led the suit, joined by Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Washington, all Democratic-led.

Four states — Massachusetts, New York, Connecticut and Minnesota — had held out but concluded that fighting on without California was not worth the expense, Bloomberg reported.

Bonta told reporters that protecting jobs was a major concern in his handling of the case and acknowledged that many people may be disappointed with his decision to strike a deal.

“My job as attorney general is to look at the facts and look at the law, weigh the options in front of us, and make the best decisions for the people of California,” he said.

Bonta said the settlement includes a commitment that the merged studio would produce 30 movies in each of the first two years of the deal, and 32 movies in each of the following three years.

At least four of those films must be independent productions, and at least 20 percent must be blockbusters, Bonta said.

The terms include a financial penalty if Paramount fails to meet the targets.

According to a joint court filing, the deal also requires at least $300 million more in annual spending on US film production by Paramount and Warner Bros. than in 2025.

The companies must also keep both studios’ production lots, honor labor agreements and commit funds to workforce training, the filing said.

It also creates a News Editorial Independence Board to set editorial principles for the combined company’s news channels, including CNN.

Compliance would be overseen by an internal monitor, an independent trustee and a committee of five states, with the court retaining jurisdiction over enforcement.

news.title: Oil price dips below $100 per barrel
news.text:
NEW YORK: Oil prices eased on Monday to their lowest level in 12 days, as investors hoped for diplomatic progress on the Iran war due to this week’s United Nations meeting and eyed a partial recovery in shipments from Saudi Arabia.

The Brent crude futures November contract fell to its lowest since September 9 at $99.51 a barrel at 1:16 p.m. ET (1716 GMT), down $4.36, or 4.2pc.

The WTI October contract that is expiring on Tuesday fell $5.30, or 5.28pc, to $95 a barrel. The November contract stood at $91.68.

On Sunday, Iran and the US exchanged new threats, although Presi-dent Donald Trump said he would be open to meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezes-hkian, who is expected to be in New York this week for the United Nations General Assembly.

Investors are pinning their hopes on a breakthrough in peace talks this week, said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates.

“Just a couple days ago that would have seemed like a very far-flung idea,” said Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho. “It’s a move in the right direction.” Iran has conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in negotiations, Al Jazeera reported, citing Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.

China has asked Iran to help rein in the Houthis after an appeal to Beijing by Saudi Arabia following the attacks, according to three Iranian sources familiar with the matter.

The attacks by the Houthis on Aramco’s East-West pipeline have prompted the firm to increase exports through the Strait of Hormuz this month and next after halting some shipments via Yanbu.

news.title: Xi due in US tomorrow for talks with Trump
news.text:
BEIJING: China’s leader Xi Jinping will visit the United States this week for talks with President Donald Trump, Beijing confirmed on Monday, expressing hope they will strengthen “strategic stability” between the world’s two largest economies.

Washington had already made clear that the leaders would meet in a bid to find common ground on trade disputes, artificial intelligence and broader strategic issues, including the Iran war.

Xi will make a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday, a Chinese government statement said.

Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said the two leaders would “have an in-depth exchange of views on major issues concerning China-US relations and world peace and development”.

 NYT report claims US agrees to extend trade tariff truce by six months though China sought longer extension

Beijing would “work with the US to enrich the substance of the relationship of constructive strategic stability between China and the US... (and) properly manage differences”, he added.

Trump will personally welcome Xi at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday before their mee-tings the following day, a US official confirmed.

“I’ll be discussing almost everything with him,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One.

According to the New York Times, the US has agreed to extend trade tariff truce by six months though China has pushed for a longer extension of the current trade truce. 

The simmering trade war between the two countries is a key concern: while both sides have maintained a tariff truce for nearly a year, they have yet to secure a lasting agreement.

Vice Premier He Lifeng, China’s top negotiator for trade, is in the United States for meetings with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

The two discussed creating a communication channel for AI concerns when they met at the weekend.

Warnings of AI apocalypse

Warnings of an AI apocalypse have hung heavy over the upcoming meeting, as both countries race for technological supremacy.

“The US has proposed that we have a notification mechanism between the two countries,” Bessent said.

Such notifications are for potential “incidents”, or a situation “that rises up to a national security level from AI”, he said.

Trump’s war on Iran casts a long shadow too, as China seeks to avoid US sanctions against countries dealing with Tehran.

China is one of Iran’s top economic partners and diplomatic backers, buys much of Tehran’s oil output and has sought to mediate in the war that has entered its seventh month.

However, analysts caution that expectations for the Trump-Xi summit are low.

news.title: Trump was a 'caged lion' roaring to return to WHCA Dinner ballroom after shooting, Leavitt says
news.text: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt revealed new details on President Donald Trump’s behind-the-scenes response after shots were fired at the White House Correspondents' Association Dinner in April. Leavitt said in a new episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" that Trump was behaving like a caged animal and was adamant about returning to the ballroom, despite having just narrowly escaped from an alleged assassination attempt. "He was like a caged lion backstage, like just roaring to get out, like, 'We gotta go back out there,’" she said. "And I'm sitting there like, ‘I don't know if I want to go back out there.’" TRUMP ADMITS HE 'WASN'T MAKING IT THAT EASY' FOR SECRET SERVICE DURING WHCD SHOOTING Minutes after the WHCA Dinner began at the Washington Hilton, a gunman, later identified as Cole Allen of Torrance, Calif., allegedly stormed the hotel while armed with weapons. Trump and Vice President JD Vance were quickly escorted out of the ballroom by members of the Secret Service. Allen, who was quickly apprehended by Secret Service agents, allegedly wrote in a manifesto that his targets were Trump administration officials except for FBI Director Kash Patel. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING: TIMELINE TRACES HOW SUSPECT’S ALLEGED CROSS-COUNTRY PLAN UNFOLDED Guests dived under tables as the gala, meant to celebrate White House correspondents, descended into chaos. Yet, Leavitt said, the president was eager to return to the ballroom and willing to wait hours for the event to resume. "[Trump] really was asking hard questions of his detail, like, ‘Why can't I go? I will wait all night. I don't care if it's 3 in the morning, get it started,’" Leavitt shared. The former White House spokeswoman said officials even began making preparations to resume the dinner as she described Trump’s impatience to make a public statement immediately after the incident. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS' DINNER SHOOTING SHARPENS FOCUS ON TRUMP’S BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION PROPOSAL "[Trump] wanted to say something and the best way to say it was in the briefing room. And we did," Leavitt said. Trump held a news conference at the White House later that night alongside top administration members, recounting how the shooting unfolded. news.title: Sylvester Stallone reveals what he said to Trump after surprise Hollywood ambassador appointment
news.text: Sylvester Stallone revealed that he was blindsided when President Donald Trump announced his appointment as a special ambassador to Hollywood. Days before his second inauguration in January 2025, Trump shared a post on his platform Truth Social in which he named Stallone, Mel Gibson and Jon Voight as "Special Envoys," describing the role as a way for the three actors to serve as his "eyes and ears" in Hollywood and advise him on efforts to bring film and television production back to the U.S. During a recent interview with The Sunday Times, the 80-year-old "Rocky" star recalled that he found out about the appointment while watching television. SYLVESTER STALLONE'S 'TULSA KING' SEASON 4 TEASER SPARKS FAN FRENZY: 'THE KING IS BACK!' "I was watching TV one night, and they go, ‘So Stallone and Mel Gibson and Jon Voight will be …’ And I went, ‘What?’ I said, ‘Excuse me? Really?’ Because if they had asked me in the beginning, I would have said, ‘This is not possible,'" Stallone said. Stallone told the outlet that he was hesitant about taking on the role because he didn't believe it was feasible. When asked if he had reservations after Trump's announcement, Stallone said, "Yes. Yes, because Hollywood, I guess it’s like feudal states." 'AMERICAN IDOL' DITCHES HOLLYWOOD FOR GEORGIA AFTER TWO DECADES AS CALIFORNIA LOSES ANOTHER PRODUCTION "They have their little kingdoms," he continued. "You don’t go in and tell six studios how to do things. And Mel Gibson and Jon Voight, we’re kind of do-our-own-thing people. No, it won’t work." The "Tulsa King" star recalled that he later explained his reasoning to Trump. "I said thank you and ciao, because it’s impossible," Stallone said. "Hollywood works, and it will evolve." "It’s corporate, and corporate people won’t want to hear me tell them about finance," he added. 'I PLAY ROCKY' REVIVES THE GAMBLE THAT MADE SYLVESTER STALLONE A SUPERSTAR In his original post on Jan. 16, 2025, Trump wrote, "It is my honor to announce Jon Voight, Mel Gibson, and Sylvester Stallone, to be Special Ambassadors to a great but very troubled place, Hollywood, California." "They will serve as Special Envoys to me for the purpose of bringing Hollywood, which has lost much business over the last four years to Foreign Countries, BACK—BIGGER, BETTER, AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!" he continued. "These three very talented people will be my eyes and ears, and I will get done what they suggest. It will again be, like The United States of America itself, The Golden Age of Hollywood!" DWAYNE 'THE ROCK' JOHNSON REJECTS HOLLYWOOD’S POLITICAL OBSESSION, BLASTS CELEBRITY ATTACK CULTURE At the time, Gibson, 70, shared that he was caught off-guard by Trump's announcement and did not have previous knowledge about his presidential appointment. "I got the tweet at the same time as all of you and was just as surprised," he told Variety in January 2025. "Nevertheless, I heed the call. My duty as a citizen is to give any help and insight I can." "Any chance the position comes with an Ambassador’s residence?" Gibson joked. Though Stallone may not have been onboard with his role as a special Hollywood ambassador, the action star appears to have a friendly relationship with Trump and heaped praise on the president during a speech following his victory in the November 2024 election. Days after the election, Stallone introduced Trump at the America First Policy Institute Gala held at the president-elect's Mar-A-Lago Club in Palm Beach, Florida. "We’re in the presence of a really mythical character," Stallone said of Trump. "I love mythology. And this individual does not exist on this planet. Nobody in the world could have pulled off what he pulled off, so I’m in awe." "When George Washington defended his country, he had no idea that he was gonna change the world," he added. "Because without him, you could imagine what the world would look like. Guess what? We got the second George Washington." Stallone was later selected as a 2025 Kennedy Center honoree, with Trump personally naming him among that year’s recipients alongside George Strait, KISS, Gloria Gaynor and Michael Crawford. The actor has backed Republicans, including John McCain and Trump, but his political history has not been strictly partisan. Over the years, Stallone has made financial contributions to both political parties, donating to various Democratic candidates and committees, including former President Joe Biden and the Democratic National Committee, as well as Republican campaigns. Meanwhile, Voight, who is a staunch supporter of Trump, appears to have embraced his role as a special ambassador. He has met with the White House and advocated for policies aimed at bringing film and TV production back to the U.S., especially a federal film tax incentive. Voight has been working with his manager Steven Paul and Paul’s associate Scott Karol as part of his push. He said meetings were being set up with leaders of both parties and urged Republicans and Democrats to "immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America." news.title: Democrats warn they are running out of money and can’t keep up with Trump before the midterms
news.text:
Democratic officials and strategists across the country are raising concerns that a significant cash shortage could prevent the party from capitalizing on favorable political conditions in the November midterms. 

According to ad-tracking data from AdImpact, Republicans are scheduled to spend $682 million on advertising from Monday through Election Day across all House and Senate races nationwide. By contrast, Democrats have reserved $491 million, giving the GOP a clear financial advantage in key battlegrounds.

The funding disparity is particularly noticeable in specific high-profile races. 

In the Texas Senate contest, Republicans are on track to outspend Democrats by more than 8-to-1 through Election Day. In New Hampshire, GOP groups have booked $24 million in ad time compared to $15 million for Democrats. And in an upstate New York House race held by Republican Representative Mike Lawler, GOP reserves total $14.3 million compared to $1.7 million from Democrats.

The financial gap has forced Democratic leaders to step up fundraising efforts, traveling to donor-rich areas like New York to solicit emergency funding. Insiders increasingly anticipate that billionaire Michael Bloomberg may step in with major financial support late in the race, as reported by CNN. 

Inside the House Democratic caucus, leadership has increased pressure on members to contribute. 

During a recent internal strategy meeting, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and his team announced an additional $2 million commitment, while individual lawmakers pledged amounts ranging from $10,000 to $250,000. Representative Susie Lee suggested tying committee assignments to financial contributions.

“If you want to see a gavel in your hand, you should be feeling some pain and putting some money in and helping us get the majority,” Lee said. 

By contrast, a closed-door meeting hosted by Vice President JD Vance for House Republicans generated roughly $20 million, a person briefed on the fundraising totals told CNN. 

Despite the spending gap, senior Democrats express confidence in their ability to win, citing economic concerns and low public approval ratings for Donald Trump. 

“We will have the money necessary to defend all of our battleground incumbents and at the same period of time, make sure we flip enough seats to take back the House of Representatives and more,” Jeffries told the outlet. “Republicans are desperate right now.”

However, local campaign officials warn that unmatched spending could alter outcomes.

“Unless more resources come in in support for House Democrats, we will ultimately leave seats on the table,” Mike Smith, leader of the primary House Democratic super PAC, told CNN.
