news.title: Arizona senator exits Hobbs probe after conflict of interest questions
news.text:
An Arizona senator has stepped back from a fourth investigation of Gov. Katie Hobbs and her ties to a state contractor after The Arizona Republic questioned the senator's work to help elect Rep. Andy Biggs, Hobbs' political opponent this November.

Sen. Jake Hoffman, a Queen Creek Republican, handed off the investigation on Sept. 21, five days after he announced it and before many of the subpoenas he warned about could be served.

He will no longer be involved, Hoffman said, and the inquiry will proceed under the oversight of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Committee Chair David Farnsworth and Hoffman chose former Arizona Supreme Court Justice Andrew Gould to oversee the investigation as special counsel, according to Senate GOP spokesperson Kim Quintero.

Still, Hoffman's involvement has deepened conflict of interest questions related to his political consulting work, and uncertainty remains about whether the investigation can escape the partisan shadow cast over how it began. One government ethics expert described a high bar for restoring its credibility.

Hoffman did not acknowledge what critics called a conflict between between his work leading the Senate Government Committee, which gives him subpoena power, and the political consulting and advertising businesses he runs. He has said he could separate the jobs.

He blamed "the corrupt political media" for a "predetermined political narrative" because The Republic asked him about the over $1 million he has been paid this year to help elect Biggs. Did he have a conflict?

"I did not, no," Hoffman told The Republic in a brief interview on Sept. 21. He referred further comment to Quintero or Farnsworth and abruptly hung up the phone.

Newer disclosures show Hoffman's companies were paid even more than previously reported. Turning Point PAC paid Hoffman's advertising companies over $350,000 to help Biggs in the two days before he announced the investigation of Hobbs on Sept. 16.

This year alone, Hoffman's companies have been paid more than $1.5 million to help Biggs defeat Hobbs in November, state disclosures show.

The Senate's investigation will scrutinize allegations, first reported in mid-2024, that a major donor to Hobbs' political operation pushed for and received a special rate increase from the Department of Child Safety in 2023. The company, Sunshine Residential Homes, had not made political contributions in Arizona in the decade before it began supporting Hobbs.

Hobbs and a former DCS director who approved the rate hike have said the governor was not involved. An investigation by Attorney General Kris Mayes found no evidence to support a charge bribery.

But Biggs and his allies have sought to keep the ties in the public spotlight, accusing Hobbs of corruption. Now, the Senate is joining the scrutiny with Election Day just over six weeks away.

Shifting the investigation appears to have scrambled its opening steps. Hoffman carried paper copies of subpoenas for Hobbs, Mayes and their aides during his Sept. 16 news conference, but most people named said they never received them or they were withdrawn days later. And a hearing set for Sept. 29 has been canceled.

“After political consultant Jake Hoffman was exposed for profiting from these shameless attacks on behalf of the Biggs campaign, partisan extremists are now scrambling to keep this taxpayer-funded sham alive," Hobbs campaign spokesperson Michael Beyer said in a statement.

Questions over Hoffman's day job, Capitol work

Hoffman's dual role raised a red flag and deserved more scrutiny so the public could be confident the investigation wasn't conducted for his own financial gain, according to Davina Hurt. Hurt is the director of government ethics at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University. 

“These are substantial payments arriving days before the subpoenas were announced,” Hurt said. “And that doesn't prove anything about the motive, again, but it makes the appearance problem hard to dismiss.” 

Conflict of interest rules exist to assure the public that officials aren't acting for their own financial benefit and that government oversight is credible, she said.

Public officers and state agency employees and their relatives aren't supposed to be a part of any financial deal with the state if they have a "substantial interest" in it, and the potential conflict also should be made public.

“The investigation launched with a paid political operative at the center,” Hurt said. “That first impression with the public can't be recalled. But there are ways to mitigate."

She said Hoffman should not have been involved in helping to select Gould if the investigation is intended to move forward independently. His involvement could further the perception that the subsequent investigation was just handed off to an ally. 

“The credibility damage can be limited ... but only with real barriers and real independence and announcements alone won’t do that,” Hurt said. 

Farnsworth has endorsed Biggs' campaign and is related to Biggs by marriage, Republic reporting has previously shown. He did not respond to a voicemail seeking comment, but Gould pledged to conduct an independent review.

"This investigation will be conducted dispassionately and according to the law, with respect for individual rights, due process, and a disciplined review of the evidence," Gould said in a statement.

Another investigation at taxpayer expense

Gould will be paid for his work as the Senate's special counsel, though it was not immediately clear how much. Quintero did not say, and the Senate did not respond to a public records request submitted Sept. 21 seeking more details. Quintero said Hoffman began the conversation about transferring the investigation.

Hiring a special counsel will drive up the cost of the Senate's new investigation, even as three others have been started or are underway.

House Republicans hired a Trump-connected firm earlier this year to investigate and seek policy changes to prevent corruption and the appearance of it, the stated goal of the Senate's work. Maricopa County Attorney Rachel Mitchell and the Arizona Auditor General are also investigating, with no publicized timelines for completing their work.

"No factual or policy conclusion should be predetermined," Gould said. "The evidence will determine where this investigation leads, and which reforms if any are ultimately recommended to the Committee."

Gould served on the Arizona Supreme Court from 2017 to 2021, when he resigned to run as a Republican for attorney general. He was named to the court by former Gov. Doug Ducey, a Republican.

Richie Taylor, a spokesperson for Mayes' office, called on the Senate to disclose how much the review would cost.

"Hoffman clearly has a conflict of interest here," Taylor said. "He didn't disclose until he was asked by the media at his press conference the payments he had received from Turning Point and I think that is clearly a conflict of interest and now they're trying to backtrack because of that."

Hoffman's businesses raise concern

Hoffman's political activity drew questions from ethics experts even before he launched the probe into the governor.

Hoffman has downplayed the ethics questions. He told The Republic in September he is subjected to a double standard, since most Arizona lawmakers have a second job in addition to their part-time work at the Legislature, and that only a fraction of his companies' revenues become his personal salary.

"We build campaigns for candidates and causes who defend the forgotten men and women of this country," he previously told The Republic. "I am proud of my team's incredible work."

It's not unheard of for politicians to do campaign or even lobbying work. But the scale of the activity is unusual for a sitting public official, a campaign finance expert previously told The Republic.

His book of business relies heavily on candidates endorsed by Turning Point, an organization he used to help lead as a spokesperson.

One company owned by Hoffman has collected $120,000 from Arizona superintendent of public instruction candidate Kimberly Yee, $88,000 from secretary of state candidate Alex Kolodin, and $4,000 from James Rogers, a lawyer with ties to President Donald Trump who is running for the state House. All three candidates are also endorsed by Turning Point.

The same company has collected almost $40,000 supporting Kolodin, Yee, Arizona attorney general candidate and Senate President Warren Petersen, and treasurer candidate Elijah Norton through independent campaigns run by Turning Point's campaign wing.

news.title: Trump inaugurates new White House helipad, but networks skip coverage during First Amendment fight (World)
news.text:
Trump inaugurates new White House helipad, but networks skip coverage during First Amendment fight

Networks skip Trump event

President Donald Trump showed off his new White House helicopter landing pad on Monday, attempting to brush aside a First Amendment firestorm even as major television networks kept their cameras away because CNN wasn't allowed to cover the event.

Trump used oversized gold scissors to cut a red, white and blue ribbon. He then exchanged handshakes with officials wearing green construction smocks and hardhats — seeking to portray business as usual.

The noise of his waiting helicopter meant Trump didn't answer shouted questions before climbing aboard Marine One for a flight to New York.

MS Now, Politico and CNN have sued after Trump announced Friday that he was banning them from covering the White House in a clear escalation of Trump’s long-running efforts — in the courts and through administrative action — to restrict news coverage he finds objectionable.

CNN normally participates in a five-network rotation that provides pooled coverage of daily events at the White House.

When it was barred from taking its customary spot on Monday, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News agreed collectively to the extraordinary step of skipping Trump's helipad ceremony.

Trump has long crowed about how the new helipad — featuring extensive granite that the president boasts will have “million-year life,” as well as a large insignia reading the “Seal of the President of the United States” — would impress Chinese President Xi Jinping, who arrives Wednesday for a state visit.

He's been focused on wowing Xi even as he decried Democrats as communists in an attempt to help Republicans retain control of Congress in upcoming midterm elections. But his effort to curb access for media outlets to the White House has overshadowed Trump's pet building projects and Xi's visit.

It has also eclipsed Trump's plans to use the helipad to fly from the White House to Joint Base Andrews and then on to New York, where he will attend the United Nations General Assembly beginning on Tuesday.

The president has ignited constitutional questions over media access, and spent large swaths of his presidency focused on building projects, even as the war in Iran rages and his approval ratings sinks now with only about six weeks before Election Day, where voters are increasingly worried about inflation and a potentially weakening economy.

Whether Trump's work will be long-lasting is unclear

Trump claims about the granite's longevity may also yet prove suspect. He long suggested that his refurbishing of the Lincoln Memorial’s Reflecting Pool would last a century — only for the paint to fade and its liner to peel away in chunks just days after it was laid.

The helipad work began in June. Trump also ripped out the original Tennessee flagstone along the West Wing’s colonnade and replaced it with black granite and refurbished with white granite the traditional walkway from the White House’s diplomatic entrance along with a portion of the asphalt driveway around the South Lawn.

Trump rushed to finish the project before Xi arrives and argues that visiting dignitaries will likely be dazzled by the project — even though Marine One is the only aircraft that lands so close to the White House.

The president says the improvement was required since Vietnam War-era choppers that long had been used as Marine One are being replaced by modern ones that are too potent to land on the White House lawn without damaging the lawn's grass.

Trump said in July that the helipad project would be privately funded and estimated its cost at up to $6 million. He’s also talked about making additional changes, however — including extensive efforts to level the ground around the helipad, that have made calculating the exact expenditure difficult.

news.title: Flights disrupted across the US Northeast due to technical problems at a key air traffic center (World)
news.text:
Flights disrupted across the US Northeast due to technical problems at a key air traffic center

Major flight disruptions

Hundreds of flights were canceled in the U.S. Northeast due to technical problems at a key regional air traffic control center, hitting every major airport in the New York City area for several hours Monday before the federal transportation chief said damaged data lines were fixed and operations were resuming.

The primary communications line failed at a key Federal Aviation Administration facility in Philadelphia and the backup fiber optic line was inadvertently severed by railroad construction workers. That left controllers without radar or communications during the day.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an online post that the primary and backup lines were fixed by Monday evening and all airports in the Northeast were operating again. But significant delays were expected to continue through the evening hours.

Hundreds of flights were canceled at the Newark, LaGuardia, Kennedy and Philadelphia airports. By Monday evening, flights were resuming at all those airports. Some airlines were allowing customers to change flights without charge. The FAA advised travelers to check the status of their flights before heading to the airport.

The outage happened just as President Donald Trump and numerous foreign leaders were flying into New York City for the United Nations General Assembly.

The technical problems stem from the same FAA facility in Philadelphia that caused numerous disruptions at Newark Liberty International Airport in the spring of 2025.

Regional control centers like these have two lines that carry radar and communications data in and out: the primary and the backup. The FAA said a circuit on the primary failed Monday morning, and when the system tried to switch to the backup, workers discovered that the fiber optic line had been cut.

Earlier in the day, Duffy said an Amtrak construction crew was to blame. Amtrak, however, pointed to a New Jersey Transit construction crew that was working in the area between Newark and New Brunswick, New Jersey.

FAA administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters earlier that the agency had focused efforts on fixing the primary connection as soon as possible by installing a new circuit on the primary line, while also working to repair the backup fiber optic line. Verizon said at the time that its technicians were also working to restore service as soon as possible.

Bedford earlier described the fiber break as “massive,” saying it would take several hours to repair, according to a video posted online by a CBS transportation reporter.

The primary circuit that failed is due to be replaced as part of the overhaul of the nation’s air traffic control system.

Also Monday, the FAA began testing a new computer system that uses AI to help predict schedule conflicts and weather issues to help air traffic controllers reroute traffic. But that system is initially being tested only in the Washington, D.C., area, so it did not appear to be linked to the outages.

news.title: Ukraine war briefing: Sanctions must continue, EU’s top diplomat stresses, as Russian attacks kill five
news.text:
The EU’s top diplomat has urged member countries to maintain sanctions targeting Russia, as Moscow’s forces continued their attacks on Ukraine, killing at least five people. “Sanctions are a core pillar of our response to Russia’s war”, Kaja Kallas told reporters in New York after a meeting of EU foreign affairs ministers. Officials aimed to close talks on a rollover of Russia sanctions soon and have the extension take place swiftly, she said. “We need to have this stability,” with sanctions remaining in place for a longer time, Kallas added on the sidelines of the UN general assembly. She stressed the EU’s position has not changed: “That’s why we are also working on a new package of sanctions.”

Discussions on the sanctions are ongoing as some EU member states sought to remove certain individuals from the bloc’s blacklist. EU countries failed on Monday to finalise a deal that involved lifting sanctions on Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman. Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiga denounced the move to remove them as “unacceptable” and said it would send Moscow the “wrong signal”. Negotiations are set to continue in Brussels in efforts to extend sanctions on almost 3,000 other individuals and entities over the war as the bloc scrambles to reach a deal ahead of late Tuesday’s deadline.

Russian forces continued their attacks on different ⁠Ukrainian regions along the 1,200km frontline on ⁠Monday, killing ​at least five people, regional officials said. Prosecutors in ⁠north-eastern Kharkiv region said a drone strike on the town of ⁠Lozova killed one person and ​injured three. Farther south ‌in Dnipropetrovsk region, ‌a drone killed a car driver ‌in Nikopol. In the Donetsk ‌region, a Russian ​strike badly damaged an apartment building in the strategic Kramatorsk, killing one person, while another person was killed in ⁠a nearby village. A sustained attack ​on ​a village in ​Mykolaiv region killed a ​three-year-old ​child. The attacks could not be independently verified. Russian also bombarded Zaporizhzhia overnight to Monday, hitting apartment blocks, a university and a shopping mall, among other sites, and wounding five people, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Donald Trump is expected to press the Ukrainian president on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, Andrew Roth reports. It comes as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine. Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, and the US president said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage he said was being exacerbated by the Ukraine war.

Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine, officials said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections. Luke Harding reports that the pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures, further consolidating Vladimir Putin’s grip on power.

Escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, UN investigators have warned, expressing fear of a repeat of last winter’s suffering. In a fresh update, the UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine warned the attacks raised concerns that already difficult living conditions could worsen dramatically with the arrival of winter, as was the case last year. Last winter, Russian forces “continued to launch systematic waves of attacks against Ukraine’s critical energy infrastructure as temperatures plunged to minus 20C”, it said in a statement. “Millions of civilians endured prolonged power outages, shortages or lengthy absence of heating.”

news.title: Trump just took an axe to his 'obsession' as press ban fallout intensifies: expert
news.text:
President Donald Trump just took an axe to one of his obsessions with his attempt to fight back against media coverage that he doesn't like. 

Last Friday, Trump revoked the press credentials of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, citing negative news coverage of his economy and the war in Iran. The fallout of that move continued to ripple on Monday, as the major news networks banded together and refused to send pool reporters to the White House. The result was an embarrassing incident during a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House, where cameras could not hear the president speaking because of the noise. 

David Rothkopf, a former international trade staffer in the Clinton administration, argued during a new episode of "The Daily Beast Podcast" that the move is sure to backfire, and it may even make Trump question whether he exists. 

“I think if Trump stopped being covered — if this media blackout, this boycott kicked in—he would start wondering about his own existence,” Rothkopf said. “I think he doesn’t believe he exists unless he reads or sees about himself on TV.”

“He wants to be the center of attention. All he wants in life is to be on TV. It’s his obsession,” Rothkopf continued. “How long before Trump folds on all of this? Because [the networks] didn’t say they’re not providing coverage today; they said they’re not providing coverage indefinitely, and there is no plan for replacement coverage.”

 Venezuelan shot by ICE agent in Texas detained with bullet inside him — lawyer 







AUSTIN, United States (AFP) — A Venezuelan shot and wounded by a United States (US) immigration agent in Texas was jailed with the bullet still inside his body, his lawyer said Monday.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, is in stable condition after suffering a gunshot wound to his torso, according to the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The shooting in Austin, Texas, on Sunday marked the latest instance of violence by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents tasked with enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Garces Perez’s attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, told a press conference that her client was transferred from a hospital to a detention centre in Pearsall, some 135 miles (215 kilometres) southwest of Austin.

“He was shot here in his back, and they didn’t take the bullet out, and they didn’t give him pain medication, and they transferred him to ICE, to a processing centre where he spent the night without a bed,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

She said Garces Perez was making a DoorDash delivery when an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.

“He didn’t know it was ICE and he did a U-turn,” she said. “The truck chased him, and sideswiped him again, and the agents came out and shot him in the back of the neck and pulled him out of the car.”

“There is absolutely zero justification for having shot him,” she said. “This is why we’re calling for a stop to ICE traffic stops. ICE officers are over-armed, overpaid, undertrained, and violent.”

DHS said on X that Garces Perez had “illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal.”

But Lincoln-Goldfinch maintained he was in the US “legally with a work permit.”

A makeshift shrine with flowers, candles, and a sign reading “Justice 4 Wilber” was placed near the site where the shooting occurred.

Trump campaigned for president on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants, and has taken a series of dramatic actions since returning to the White House.

Nearly 51,000 undocumented migrants were arrested in the United States in August, according to DHS figures.

Ruben Ray Martinez, 23, was shot by ICE in March 2025, in what the Texas Tribune said was the first known killing by immigration agents of an American in Trump’s second term.

More recently, a Mexican man named Lorenzo Salgado died in July after he was shot by an ICE officer in Houston, Texas.

news.title: Panic drove NYC and LA to ban school AI — and that’s a big mistake
news.text:
There are two ways for America’s schools to get artificial intelligence wrong.

One is to hand a child a chatbot and let it do all the thinking — and the other is to ban AI and pretend it doesn’t exist.

New York and Los Angeles have both chosen the second option.

That means they’re setting their students up to get the first.

Americans are split when it comes to AI, as evidenced by the debate that raged last week.

When the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI urged AI companies to slow development down, President Donald Trump dubbed their alarm bell a “sick conspiracy” — and skeptics saw self-interest behind both warnings.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani faulted Trump for what he called a “very flip response” to AI companies’ talk of “the end of humanity,” and the New York City Council has called for an all-member hearing to question AI companies about the dangers.

The nation is somewhere in between: A Politico poll this month found that 48% want to pause the development of advanced AI. 

Yet on Sept. 2, Mamdani and Chancellor Kamar Samuels chose to go to extremes, banning generative AI in NYC public schools for every student from 2-K through grade 8 — about 600,000 kids.

Later that same day, Los Angeles blocked AI on school devices in every grade — banning it indefinitely for more than 378,000 students.

These school systems are behaving as if a kindergartener’s educational needs are the same as a 13-year-old’s, or a 17-year-old’s.

But their bans fail no matter who is right about AI.

If Trump is right and AI is the engine of the future economy, our students must learn how to use it.

If Mamdani is right and AI is dangerous, students must learn how it works, so they can understand its flaws and pitfalls.

Either way the answer is to teach — and a ban teaches nothing.

Mamdani calls his policy a moratorium. But a moratorium only works if the world outside is also pausing, and right now it isn’t.

More than half of US teens already use chatbots for schoolwork, according to Pew, and one in 10 students say a chatbot does most of it. 

So students with AI access at home will learn through trial and error, not through careful instruction.

And the rules don’t bind private schools, charter schools or tutors, nor do they touch what happens at home or across the rest of the country.

That means students without access will fall behind.

Consequently, New York’s and LA’s moratoriums aren’t taking AI away from kids — just stripping them of the opportunity to learn from teachers how to ask AI good questions, evaluate its information, and gauge the trustworthiness of its assertions.

This isn’t to say students at every level should have access to AI in school.

For the youngest students, through second grade, the ban is correct: They must learn to read first.

However, beginning in third grade students should be taught to read what AI produces, spot weak claims, and distinguish fact from opinion.

Too many students today can’t do that.

When Stanford researchers tested 3,446 high school students in 2019, two-thirds of them could not tell a news story from an ad, even when the ad was labeled. 

Early research shows that this kind of work can improve critical-thinking skills.

By middle school, a student needs to be able to trace an AI’s claim back to a real source and spot a citation that doesn’t exist — a skill that takes years to teach. 

Yet the nation’s two largest school districts have no plan to change their teaching to include what students should learn about AI at different grade levels, or when.

That’s outright negligence.

As I’ve argued in a Manhattan Institute brief, students need a real AI-literacy curriculum, one that teaches them to judge what AI produces so it never does the thinking for them.

Regarding AI as a tool, rather than a threat to learning, is key: More than a third of entry-level jobs already require AI literacy.

That’s also what a cautious public is asking for.

Americans are not telling schools to hand children over to a chatbot — but neither are they telling schools to pretend AI doesn’t exist.

A curriculum that keeps AI out of the earliest grades, puts the teacher in charge in third grade and builds real skills by middle school respects that caution and still prepares students to succeed.

Students are already using AI, whether the two largest school districts like it or not. 

We can teach them how to use it well — or leave a million kids to just figure it out on their own. 

Jennifer Weber is a fellow at the Manhattan Institute.
news.summary: Major school systems are behaving as if a kindergartener’s educational needs are the same as a 13-year-old’s, or a 17-year-old’s. But their bans fail no matter who is right about AI.
news.author: Jennifer Weber

news.title: US threatens secondary sanctions over services to Iranian airlines
news.text:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned that Iranian airlines could be effectively shut out of international travel from Wednesday (local time), on September 23, as Washington threatens secondary sanctions against foreign companies that continue providing services to Iran’s carriers.

According to Al Jazeera, Bessent said on Monday that “on September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world,” as the Trump administration steps up economic pressure on Tehran.

The warning extends beyond Iranian airlines to foreign airports, fuel suppliers, ticketing companies and other businesses involved in supporting the carriers’ international operations.

“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said, according to Al Jazeera.

Latest threat expands US sanctions campaign

The latest threat comes amid the Trump administration’s broader sanctions campaign aimed at restricting Iran’s access to international financial and commercial networks.

Earlier this month, the US Treasury imposed sanctions on Iranian airlines that had not previously been targeted, along with companies outside Iran accused of supporting Iran’s aviation sector.

Iran’s aviation industry has already faced significant restrictions due to years of US sanctions, which have limited Iranian carriers’ ability to purchase new aircraft and obtain spare parts and maintenance services.

The latest measures form part of a wider US sanctions regime targeting Iran’s economy, including its energy, shipping, technology, gold and digital-asset sectors. Secondary sanctions can expose foreign businesses dealing with sanctioned Iranian entities to restrictions on their access to the US financial system.

Washington seeks Chinese cooperation on Iran sanctions

Bessent’s comments came a day after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, ahead of a planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

China is among Iran’s key economic partners and diplomatic supporters, making Beijing’s cooperation significant to Washington’s efforts to restrict Tehran’s access to international finance.

According to Al Jazeera, Bessent said Chinese officials had been “very engaged” in discussions surrounding the US pressure campaign.

He also said Washington was holding positive discussions with Chinese financial authorities, including People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, over compliance with US sanctions targeting Iran.

Published on September 22, 2026
news.summary: The warning targets airports, fuel suppliers and ticketing companies as Washington intensifies pressure on Tehran’s international financial and commercial networks

news.title: US set for major military expansion in Greenland – Reuters
news.text:
The US is set to establish a military presence at two additional sites in Greenland under a security agreement with Denmark and the self-governing Arctic territory, according to media reports, as Copenhagen insists the deal does not surrender Danish sovereignty.

US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement at UN headquarters in New York on Tuesday, on the sidelines of the General Assembly. The full text has not yet been made public, but media reports suggest the US is seeking to expand its military footprint imminently.

Washington plans to reopen the former Cold War-era Bluie West One base at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a presence at Mestersvig on the island’s east coast, Reuters reported on Monday, citing people familiar with the negotiations.

Mestersvig is currently used by Denmark’s Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, an elite military unit tasked with reconnaissance and enforcing Danish sovereignty in the remote Arctic region. Trump has repeatedly mocked Denmark’s reliance on dog-sled patrols as evidence that Copenhagen was failing to adequately protect Greenland.

Trump has portrayed the agreement in sweeping terms, saying last week that it gives the US “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland.” He also claimed that no American adversary would be allowed to establish a base or military presence, or make sensitive investments on the island without Washington’s approval.

Denmark has stressed that the arrangement does not transfer sovereignty over Greenland to the United States.

Frederiksen said the agreement explicitly recognizes “the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark,” as well as the Greenlandic population’s right to self-determination. Copenhagen has presented the deal as a way of placing greater responsibility for Arctic security within NATO rather than handing control exclusively to Washington.

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen has said Copenhagen remains willing to accommodate legitimate US security interests in the Arctic while maintaining its established “red lines.”

The agreement follows months of tensions triggered by Trump’s repeated demands for US control over Greenland, during which he at times declined to rule out military or economic pressure. Copenhagen and Nuuk firmly rejected any transfer of the territory.

Washington already enjoys extensive military access under a 1951 defense agreement, amended in 2004. During the Cold War, the US operated 17 installations and stationed more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today, its presence is concentrated at Pituffik Space Base, with roughly 150 US military personnel stationed there.
news.summary:
President Trump seeks “permanent control” over security in the self-governing Danish territory under a deal to be signed Tuesday

news.title: White House launches Trump TV, 24/7 streaming platform amid media access dispute
news.text:
The White House on Monday (local time) launched “Trump TV”, a 24/7 streaming platform featuring past speeches by US President Donald Trump, administration announcements and updates, providing viewers with a dedicated platform for presidential content.

Announcing the launch, the official X account of The White House said, “IT’S LIVE. TRUMP TV IS STREAMING NOW. 24/7, updated in real time, with top past moments, announcements, and the latest and greatest from the administration all in one place. Not every big moment has made it on your tv, now it can.”

During the launch, the White House broadcast footage of Trump’s previous public appearances and speeches, including his swearing-in ceremony as the 47th President of the United States.

Launch comes amid media access dispute

The launch comes amid an escalating dispute between the Trump administration and several major news organisations over White House press access.

Earlier on Monday, Trump defended restrictions imposed on CNN, Politico and MS NOW, after the three organisations filed a federal lawsuit challenging the administration’s decision to revoke access for their journalists.

Speaking to reporters outside Gracie Mansion following his meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Trump dismissed suggestions that media organisations could boycott him.

“They said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me. So I wasn’t very worried about that. Look at all that press,” Trump said.

Trump defends restrictions on news organisations

Trump said the media had an obligation to report fairly and defended his administration’s decision to restrict outlets he accused of publishing what he called “fake news”.

“I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair. And if they’re fake news, I really think I have an obligation not to allow them into another very special house,” Trump said, referring to the White House.

The White House has defended the restrictions, arguing that the First Amendment protects the media’s right to publish but does not guarantee individual organisations access to the White House grounds, briefing room or presidential press pool.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico have challenged the restrictions in court, arguing that the government should not determine which journalists can access the White House based on their reporting.

Dispute affects White House television pool

The dispute has also affected the White House television pool, which provides shared footage of presidential events to participating news organisations.

Trump is currently in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly and is scheduled to participate in the high-level General Debate and hold meetings with several world leaders.

Published on September 22, 2026
news.summary: The new platform features presidential footage and administration updates as legal challenges over access by news organisations continue

news.title: Press-Starved Trump, 80, Announces Desperate TV Move
news.text:
President Donald Trump has launched his own television channel after banning three networks from the White House television press pool.

The announcement comes three days after the president angrily removed CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the pool because he doesn’t like their coverage. Those outlets have since sued the administration, claiming a violation of their First Amendment rights.

“Top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time. Stay informed and stay up to date!” it read.

The channel’s first stream was of the president’s speech at Mt. Rushmore on July 3. At the 20-minute mark, about 8,500 people were watching. One hour in, the channel was showing Trump’s 2025 inauguration to an audience of only 3,800. The White House’s YouTube account has 3.15 million subscribers.

The White House did not respond to specific questions from the Daily Beast about “Trump TV,” like why comments were disabled, instead linking to a post by Deputy Assistant to the President Kaelan Dorr.

“Welcome to TrumpTV,” he wrote. “The press, in some cases, reported inaccurately or not at all on the Administration’s many record breaking accomplishments on behalf of all Americans. Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration’s greatest hits, unfiltered. All on the White House YouTube Channel and Official App ENJOY!!”

After Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, several other networks—NBC, ABC, CBS, and even Fox News—united to pause White House television pool coverage. The result: Trump was inaudible, even on the White House’s own livestream on Monday.

Photographers from major wire agencies and news outlets—including The New York Times, the Associated Press, AFP, Reuters, Getty, and The Washington Post—have also paused publishing new images of the 80-year-old president.

“In solidarity with news organizations who have had their access to the White House restricted, AP joined a group of news outlets in not publishing photographs of today’s presidential events,” Patrick Maks, a spokesperson for AP, told the Daily Beast. “No news organization—or person—should be retaliated against by the government over the words they use.”

Trump had previously kicked around the idea of a television channel named after himself. In the final weeks of his 2016 campaign, the president launched a Facebook-only talk show called “Trump Tower Live.” The product was far from polished, but it contributed to chatter that the then-candidate was angling to start an actual TV channel if the election didn’t turn out in his favor, The New York Times reported at the time.

Monday’s premiere of “Trump TV” followed the launch of a White House app, where users can presumably watch the channel and be fed “the news that matters most.”

But as CNN reporter Daniel Dale noted, the app selectively presents data to support the president’s so-called “accomplishments.” Instead of showing the current average price for a gallon of gasoline, for example, the app lists the price from before Trump began his war against Iran—when it was more than $1.50 cheaper. The listed inflation rate was also from February, whereas the August rate was one percent higher.
news.summary:
Jonathan Ernst / REUTERSPresident Donald Trump has launched his own television channel after banning three networks from the White House television press pool.

The announcement comes three days after the president angrily removed CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the pool because he doesn’t like their coverage. Those outlets have since sued the administration, claiming a violation of their First Amendment rights.

“Trump TV,” the White House announced, would begin airing at 7 p.m. on Monday night and would be “streaming 24/7.” The White House’s YouTube channel described the stream as a place where people can “watch the Trump Administration’s biggest moments all in one place.”

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: World News | JFK, LaGuardia, Newark Face Ground Stops Amid FAA Equipment Outage Disrupting Flights Across US Northeast
news.text:
New York [US], September 22 (ANI): New York's John F Kennedy International Airport, LaGuardia Airport and Newark Liberty International Airport were among several airports affected by ground stops on Monday (local time) following an equipment outage at the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), disrupting flights across the Northeast.

According to flight-tracking service Flightradar24, JFK and LaGuardia were added to the list of airports where flights bound for the facilities were being held at their origin airports.

“New York airports JFK and La Guardia have now been added to the list of airports ground stopped (flights to those airports are held on the ground at their origin) due to the FAA equipment outage,” Flightradar24 said in a post on X.

"Arrivals have just resumed at Newark. No commercial flights landed at EWR between 09:38 and 17:22 local time today," Flightradar24 posted. 

Flightradar24 also reported significant disruption at Newark.

“Through 17:30 EDT, 107 diversions away from Newark (EWR) to 34 separate airports impacting 25 airlines. IAD (19) & JFK (12) took in the greatest number of flights. United (with its EWR hub) was most impacted with 70 diversions,” it said.

According to the New York Post, the disruption was linked to two equipment failures and affected more than half a dozen airports across the Northeast for much of Monday.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said a circuit failure at the Philadelphia Terminal Radar Approach Control facility resulted in the loss of radio and radar equipment serving several airports, including JFK, LaGuardia and Newark.

The outage began around 10 am and resulted in more than 1,000 flight delays or cancellations, according to the report, as New York prepared to host world leaders and ministers for the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a fibre-optic line was cut during work near an Amtrak rail line, affecting Verizon communication lines.

By 6 pm, Duffy said the telecommunications lines had been repaired and airport operations were resuming, though residual delays were expected.

“The telecom lines have been repaired, and all airport operations in the Northeast are resuming,” Duffy said.

Bedford also criticised the existing infrastructure, saying the network design needed an overhaul to prevent similar failures.

“The network design is terrible. And if we don’t fix the network design, we’re going to continue having these failures,” he said. (ANI)

news.title: Crowley visits Kewaunee Co. farm, ties Tiffany to rising diesel prices
news.text:
WEST KEWAUNEE – Clark Riemer has never gambled at a casino but considers the $500,000 he and his brother pay each year to plant corn and soybeans on their farm to have higher stakes than any table game.

He locked in a contract in January for the 6,000 gallons of diesel he would need for the year. His brother did not, believing prices would stay low, Riemer told the Green Bay Press-Gazette.

When it came time to buy fertilizer, a retailer gave him a weekend in February to decide whether to pay $540 per ton. Then the United States and Israel launched strikes against Iran. Riemer said the retailer could not get a price for nitrogen, phosphorus or pot ash the next Monday, and that any contract at $540-per-ton would not have been honored.

He considered this year the worst for farming in 35 years.

“Usually, I keep my mouth shut, but it’s to the point where I can’t no more,” Riemer said Sept. 21. “This farm could come to an end after 100-some years and all the blood, sweat and tears and everything that was put into this because of some policies, Washington, because somebody doesn’t care about people down here at the bottom.”

Farmers and families are balking at affording life’s costs, a national issue that’s weighed heavily in the race for Wisconsin governor. And with diesel prices breaking record highs day after day in Wisconsin, Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley started a statewide tour Sept. 21 to paint Republican opponent Tom Tiffany as responsible for high fuel prices, a framing Tiffany has challenged.

In Riemer’s shed with Democratic U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin, Crowley criticized Tiffany’s votes in the House of Representatives against resolutions to end the conflict in Iran, which he called “a war of choice.” He told reporters that farmers “have been left high and dry” from the continuing conflict. 

“Tiffany had five chances to end the war that is driving these prices up,” Crowley said in a Sept. 21 news release, “and five times he has chosen his boss, Donald Trump, over the people he’s supposed to represent here in Wisconsin. I’m done with the excuses.”

In a statement to the Press-Gazette, Tiffany criticized tax increases and projected budget shortfalls in Milwaukee County under Crowley’s county executive leadership as going against the spirit of affordability. Tiffany has previously cast Crowley as a tax-and-spender, calling the tax increases and deficits “disqualifying” for the governorship. He has staked his economic pitch to voters on lowering taxes, which he has said will spur growth.

“David Crowley’s answer to rising costs is to take more of your hard-earned money,” Tiffany said. “Mine is to make sure you keep more of it so you have more for groceries, more for the bills, and more left in your pocket.”

Gas price volatility, largely influenced by geopolitical conflicts, has become a political issue in the campaign for governor.

The average price for regular gas in Wisconsin sat about 3 cents lower than the national average on Sept. 21, at $4.43 per gallon, according to AAA. It was $2.90 a gallon a year ago. The average price of diesel in the state sat at $6.56 on Sept. 21, exacerbated by downed refineries in Illinois and Indiana, plus Russian bans on its diesel exports in the wake of Ukrainian attacks on refineries.

Both Tiffany and Crowley have both come out in favor of repealing the state's minimum markup law, which requires selling certain products, including gasoline, by a certain price above its wholesale price.

Tiffany has said he supports repealing the law, called the Unfair Sales Act, in its entirety, on gas, as well as on tobacco and alcohol.

Crowley has said he supports eliminating the markup on gas. At Riemer’s farm, he said the savings to customers at the pump would amount to “north of 40 cents a gallon.”

Matthew Hauser, president of the Wisconsin Fuel and Retail Association, disputed that getting rid of the law would lead to such drops in costs.

The price of crude oil is the largest mover of gasoline prices, with its costs accounting for just over half of the price of gasoline in 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Other factors include costs to distribute and market, refining costs, and federal and state taxes, underlying costs which Hauser said a repeal would not change.

He noted the law, first passed in 1939 to counter large companies undercutting smaller ones, applies to the wholesale cost of fuel, not its retail price. The law also lets gas stations sell under that floor to meet the price of competitors.

Any savings would not be immediate and would fall “well short” of the savings the candidates were touting, Hauser said.

news.title: How India turned US sanctions into a dud 25 years ago, forced their withdrawal
news.text: US President Donald Trump has signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctions Bill into law, effectively giving him the power to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries trading with Russia. The move leaves India, which sources more than half of its crude oil imports from Russia, exposed to potentially severe trade barriers in its largest export market. This, however, is hardly the first time India has found itself under the shadow of US sanctions.Exactly 25 years ago, New Delhi came out on top after facing a similar set of punitive measures imposed by Washington.The story goes back to the late 1990s, when India was in the midst of a heady transformation. The country was rapidly liberalising its long stagnant economy and opening up to the world. Economic growth was on the upswing, driven by strong foreign investment and growth of the IT and services sector. On the global stage, New Delhi's once all-weather ally, the USSR, had been consigned to history, and India was in the midst of a rapprochement with the West, especially the US.Then in 1998, the administration of then-US President Bill Clinton slapped a sanctions package on New Delhi that banned almost all foreign aid, financial assistance, military cooperation and technology transfer in a bid to clip India's ambitions to become a nuclear power. But if the sanctions were an attempt to make New Delhi toe the Washington line, they failed. On September 22, 2001, President George W Bush waived his predecessor's sanctions.As fresh US sanctions loom over New Delhi, the 1998 episode offers a useful reminder of how New Delhi dealt with Washington's pressure a quarter of a century ago.THE NUCLEAR TEST BEHIND AMERICAN SANCTIONSOn May 11, 1998, at 3.45 pm, three underground nuclear detonations were carried out at an Indian Army firing range in Rajasthan's Pokhran as part of Operation Shakti (also called Operation Pokhran-II), with then-PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee shortly thereafter announcing that India was now a full-fledged nuclear power.But while the news of the tests might have made Buddha smile, it wasn't the case in Washington DC. Caught completely unawares, America's reaction to India's entry into the nuclear club was one of disbelief and anger. According to the US State Department Archives, then-President Clinton had stated that he was "deeply disturbed by the nuclear tests", and that they were contrary to the goal "of building a safer 21st century"."This action by India not only threatens the stability of the region, it directly challenges the firm international consensus to stop the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction," Clinton had further added.An American response was thus inevitable, and it came on May 13, 1998. That day, Clinton informed the US Congress that he had imposed sanctions on India, under Section 102 of the Arms Export Control Act, also known as the Glenn Amendment Act. The aims of the sanction package, according to the State Department Archives, were to force New Delhi, among other things, to not "deploy or test missiles or nuclear weapons", and "cut off fissile material production for nuclear weapons".SANCTIONS CUT OFF FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, BLOCKED WORLD BANK FUNDING TO INDIAThe 1998 American sanctions led to the termination of all US foreign assistance except humanitarian and food aid. This cut off about $21 million in economic development assistance and $6 million earmarked for a greenhouse gas phaseout programme, as per official US government data.The US also opposed loans from global institutions such as the World Bank and IMF, blocking $3-4 billion in funding for India's infrastructure and development projects. Washington also committed American banks and government agencies to deny New Delhi any and all new loans and credit lines, except those to be used in purchasing food and agricultural commodities.Additionally, the sanctions suspended the sale of defence hardware, services, and foreign military financing under the Arms Export Control Act, directly impacting potential arms deals and cooperation.SANCTIONS FAILED TO DENT INDIA — IT GREW STRONGER OVER THE YEARSIn 1998, India was in the midst of a sweeping economic liberalisation programme, with reforms opening up the economy to greater foreign investment and international trade. The transformation began after the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, when India received substantial financing from institutions such as the IMF and World Bank while undertaking wide-ranging structural reforms.The American sanctions, thus, did have some effect. The suspension of sales of military equipment and financing was felt during the Kargil War the following year. And the blocking of funding via the World Bank and the IMF led to delays in several infrastructure and even military projects (such as the HAL Tejas project). Exports to the US also saw a dip that year.New Delhi, however, stayed the course. Then-PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee, addressing Parliament on May 27, 1998, defended the tests as a matter of national security. "The touchstone that has guided us in making the correct choice was national security," he told the Lok Sabha, insisting that India's new nuclear weapons were "weapons of self-defence" intended to ensure that the country was not subjected to "nuclear threats or coercion".Asked whether the American sanctions could impact India's economy, he told India Today Magazine, "Sanctions cannot and will not hurt us. India will not be cowed down by any such threats and punitive steps. India has the sanction of her own past glory and future vision to become strong in every sense of the term."And in many ways, India did become stronger despite the sanctions.GDP growth averaged around 6.5% in the mid-1990s due to market reforms, and by the time sanctions were imposed, the economy was stable at about 5.8%. By 2003, just 5 years after the US sanctions, India's GDP was growing by 7.8% annually. India's trade links with the world remained robust.New Delhi also diversified its trade partners during this period. The US continued to import billions of dollars' worth of textiles and gemstones while exporting machinery. The European Union imported textiles, leather, and chemicals, in return for exporting industrial equipment. Russia supplied defence hardware and bought Indian pharmaceuticals and tea. The UAE and Saudi Arabia exported oil while importing gems and rice. Japan and China also remained active partners, trading in electronics, textiles, and chemicals.In fact, then-Finance Minister Yashwant Sinha would later tell news agency PTI in 2001, "As far as the Indian economy itself was concerned, except for certain defence supplies, sanctions had no meaning."INDIA CONTINUED TO ENGAGE WITH THE US, LED TO SANCTIONS WAIVER BY BUSHMore importantly, despite being hit with sanctions, India kept up engaging with the US, enabling a gradual thaw in ties. US President Bill Clinton, who imposed the sanctions in the first place, turned up for a bilateral visit in 2000, the first such trip made by an American President to India since 1978.Finally, on September 22, 2001, exactly 25 years ago, US President George W Bush waived the sanctions, opening the door to economic and military aid. New Delhi-Washington DC ties would continue to grow over the years, boosted by India's support in the global fight against terrorism post-911. Finally, in 2008, the signing of the Indo-US nuclear deal by PM Manmohan Singh and President Bush saw Washington finally recognise India as a responsible nuclear power.A quarter of a century later, India and the US are even more intertwined than ever. The US remains the largest destination of Indian exports, accounting for 19.78% of all shipments in financial year 2025-26, while bilateral trade reached an estimated $239.6 billion in 2025.It is this massive export market under threat from US sanctions. A blanket 100% tariff would render Indian goods thoroughly uncompetitive in the American market. This is because New Delhi prioritises energy security for its 1.4 billion citizens, even if it means buying Russian crude.The lesson from 25 years ago is that India must continue to prioritise its own interests rather than bend to pressure from the US. But it must also continue engaging constructively with America. The experience of 2001 shows that even after a period of intense disagreement, sustained engagement can help rebuild ties and create a path out of confrontation.- EndsPublished By: Shounak SanyalPublished On: Sep 22, 2026 06:30 IST
news.summary: How India turned US sanctions into a dud 25 years ago, forced their withdrawal

news.title: Ken Paxton snubbed from Texas GOP fundraisers as polls spell trouble: report
news.text:
Former President George W. Bush and Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) are teaming up to raise money for Senate Republicans nationwide, but they've pointedly left one candidate off the guest list: Ken Paxton, the GOP's own Senate nominee in their home state of Texas.

Cornyn is hosting a Monday evening fundraiser in Dallas benefiting six Republican Senate candidates through a new joint committee called Maintain the Majority, according to an invitation obtained by the New York Times. Bush is attending as a "special guest." Paxton previously defeated Cornyn in a costly primary fight earlier this year, and neither he nor his campaign was included in Monday's event or would comment when asked about it.

The snub lands as Paxton continues trailing Democratic opponent James Talarico in polls and fundraising, even as outside groups aligned with President Donald Trump and Senate Republicans have committed tens of millions of dollars to advertising on his behalf across the state. Paxton has long been a divisive figure even within his own party: Texas House Republicans impeached him on corruption charges back in 2023, though the state Senate later acquitted him, and he subsequently campaigned to remove GOP lawmakers and judges who'd crossed him.

Cornyn hasn't held back criticizing his former rival publicly.

"Paxton's a poor campaigner," Cornyn told the Texas Tribune in August. "He's lazy and doesn't raise money. And he basically is not offering a very compelling case for his election."

Paxton pushed back on Fox News, insisting he works 18-hour days and that Cornyn simply doesn't know his schedule.

The rift reflects a broader civil war brewing between old-guard Bush Republicans and the Trump-aligned wing of the party that Paxton represents. Just last week, longtime Bush adviser Karl Rove announced he wouldn't vote for Texas Railroad Commission nominee Bo French over a racist social media post, prompting Trump to call Rove a "stone-cold loser" on Truth Social after Paxton declined to condemn French himself. Paxton has also previously clashed publicly with Rove and decisively defeated Bush's own nephew, George P. Bush, in the 2022 attorney general primary.

The fundraiser's host committee reads like a who's who of Bush-era Republican royalty, including former Supreme Court nominee Harriet Miers, ex-Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, and megadonor Harlan Crow, with entry requiring contributions between $1,000 and $61,500. Beneficiaries include Sens. Susan Collins, Jon Husted and Dan Sullivan, along with Senate candidates John E. Sununu, Ashley Hinson and Mike Rogers.

Notably, Paxton isn't the only Trump-backed nominee left out. Michael Whatley of North Carolina and Mike Collins of Georgia, both running in states Trump carried in 2024, were also excluded from the fundraising push, as Democrats have shown surprising polling strength in both races.

Collins campaign spokeswoman Blake Kernen confirmed the senator welcomes the establishment support, while representatives for the other beneficiaries didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

news.title: NATO will share Arctic responsibility as Greenland security deal with U.S. moves forward, Denmark says
news.text:
Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. are to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington ‌and Copenhagen. 

The agreement, to be signed at the UN General Assembly in New York at 10:30 a.m. ET on Tuesday, has not been made public. Denmark and Greenland say the deal will benefit the Arctic island and respect its sovereignty.

The deal is expected to allow the U.S., which already has one military base in Greenland, to expand its military presence to two additional sites. 

One of those sites is Narsarsuaq, whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since ​the U.S. closed its Cold War-era Bluie West One military base there in the 1950s. The other ​is Mestersvig, a military outpost currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a special forces unit that enforces Danish sovereignty in the territory, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Trilateral signing ceremony planned

U.S. President Donald Trump will meet in New York on Tuesday with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik ​Nielsen for a trilateral signing ceremony, a White House official said.

The deal follows months of pressure from Trump, who has said the U.S. should ⁠control Greenland and at times refused to ⁠rule out using military or economic force to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. His threats peaked ‌in January, triggering a diplomatic crisis within the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the military defence alliance, and pushing Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure. 

The agreement "will be in a form where responsibility for security in the Arctic is not only Danish or American," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen told national broadcaster TV2 on Sunday. He said that, to a large extent, "it would be NATO that looks after the Arctic." 

It remained unclear whether the deal ⁠amends an existing 1951 defence agreement that is the legal basis for the U.S. presence in Greenland.

"It appears that we are now using this crisis to try to strengthen NATO's cohesion through Greenland," said Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS). 

Strategic interest in Greenland

Washington's strategic interest in Greenland dates back to the Second World War. In 1941, the U.S. signed a deal with Danish envoy ‌Henrik Kauffmann, who acted without authority from his country, then under German occupation.

The U.S. sought the deal to keep Greenland out of German hands and secure the North Atlantic supply route between North America and Europe. Under the agreement, the U.S. built airfields, naval facilities and weather stations across the island, reaching around 5,500 military personnel by 1943, according to DIIS.

In 1946, then-U.S. president Harry Truman sought to buy the island as a strategic asset for $100 million US in gold, but Copenhagen declined ​to sell. Instead, a new agreement was signed in 1951 that gave the U.S. military extensive rights in Greenland but was tied to the existence of NATO.

"I don't think Denmark and Greenland will sign if the same NATO clause isn't included," ⁠said Gad.

Cold War presence

During the Cold War, the U.S. maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel in Greenland. Today only Pituffik Space Base remains, with some 150 ⁠U.S. military personnel.

A NATO spokesperson said on Saturday that the alliance welcomed the new agreement, which would "help advance security, stability and co-operation in this vital region."

Rasmussen, who travelled to ⁠New York ⁠overnight, declined to discuss the contents of the agreement. 

"But we have ​said from the start that we are open to accommodating the United States' legitimate security interests," he told Danish news agency Ritzau on Monday.

Trump says deal struck to boost U.S. military presence in GreenlandGreenland, Denmark say deal with U.S. will not cede sovereignty

Trump said in a social media post on Friday the agreement gave the U.S. "permanent control over ⁠security, and all other needs, in Greenland," and that no U.S. adversary could have a base or military presence there without Washington's written approval.

Denmark has not responded to Trump's assertion, though Copenhagen earlier acknowledged it underinvested in Greenland's defence for decades and has pledged to expand its military presence on the island, including more NATO troops.

Greenland's government has sought to reassure the public about the deal.

Erik Jensen, an opposition lawmaker in Greenland, wrote on social media that he had read the draft agreement. "I feel reassured and am not worried," he said, adding that the island's foreign minister was handling the work ⁠well.
news.summary: Denmark, Greenland and the U.S. are to sign a deal on Greenland's security on Tuesday, an agreement Denmark says will put Arctic security under NATO's watch rather than leaving it solely to Washington ‌and Copenhagen.

news.title: Vance defends Trump’s media ban
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Sep 22 (IANS) US Vice President JD Vance defended President Donald Trump’s decision to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from special access to the White House, rejecting the argument that the move amounted to an attack on free speech. “He's not banning media outlets,” Vance told reporters before travelling to North Carolina. “What he's doing is saying, ‘We're not gonna give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda.’” Vance claimed about 92 per cent of the three organisations’ stories on Trump and his administration were negative. He said such coverage did not represent the American people or public opinion. “So, if you're gonna engage in what is effectively far left propaganda, why would a Republican White House give you special access?” he asked. Pressed on how the decision squared with his past defence of free speech, Vance said the outlets remained free to report on the administration, receive public reports and speak with people inside and outside the government. “What the president has said is, ‘We're not gonna give you special access inside the White House,’” he said. Vance compared Politico’s coverage of Trump with Breitbart’s treatment of former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden. He argued that previous administrations had not been expected to grant comparable access to the conservative outlet. “It's about basic fairness,” Vance said. “They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not gonna get an office in the White House anymore.” The vice president also addressed Iran, high fuel prices and the Russia-Ukraine war. He said substantial volumes of oil and gas continued to pass through the Strait of Hormuz despite what he described as daily Iranian attacks on ships. “What the president has said is Iran can't have a nuclear weapon,” Vance said. “We're of course going to try to protect the free flow of commerce as much as we can. That's what the United States Navy has done for the past 80 years.” He declined to get ahead of Trump but said further discussions on Iran were likely during the UN General Assembly in New York this week. Asked about prospects for peace, Vance described the Russia-Ukraine war as the most difficult international conflict to resolve. He said Trump was expected to meet President Zelenskyy “either tomorrow or the day after”. “Do I think it'll get solved eventually? Yes, it's just a question of time,” he said. On elevated energy costs, Vance attributed the rise to threats against international shipping. He said the administration was trying to push prices down while seeking short-term relief for Americans. “One of the things the president has talked about is encouraging some of the states to give Americans relief from the gas taxes,” he said. Vance spoke ahead of a campaign trip to North Carolina with Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley. He said they would highlight the Trump administration’s economic agenda, including no tax on tips and overtime and what he called the most significant middle-class tax cuts in 30 years.
